O Madhusudana, is there no place from which one does not return, where this cycle of birth and death finally ceases?

Such a place is My supreme abode, Paramdham, where one, having reached it, never has to return. It is said: न तद्भासयते सूर्यो न शशाङ्को न पावकः । यद्गत्वा न निवर्तन्ते तद्धाम परमं मम ॥ Neither the sun nor the moon nor fire illuminates that abode of Mine. Those who reach it never return. The primary purpose of human birth, O Arjuna, is to attain this supreme goal, which can only be achieved through the human form. Therefore, the human body is considered the gateway to liberation (Moksha).

O Yogeshwara, you have answered many of my questions. I have heard that at the time of death, a person suffers greatly, whether it is due to a fatal wound from a weapon on the battlefield or if it comes naturally. Is there no way to make death easier?

Arjuna, the way is not to make death easier, but to attain liberation by breaking free from the cycle of life and death. If a person adopts this method that I am telling you at the time of death, he will immediately attain liberation and reach My abode.
What is that secret method, Madhava?

At the time of departing the body, stop the functions of all your senses, stabilize your mind in the heart, and establish your life-force (prana) in the brain. Remembering the Supreme Being, constantly chant the sacred syllable ॐ (Om). By doing so, no matter how sinful that person may have been throughout his life, he will surely attain liberation. As I have declared:
अपि चेत्सुदुराचारो भजते मामनन्यभाक् |
साधुरेव स मन्तव्यः सम्यग्व्यवसितो हि सः ||
(Even if one commits the most abominable action, if he is engaged in unalloyed devotional service, he is to be considered saintly because he is properly situated in his determination.)
क्षिप्रं भवति धर्मात्मा शश्वच्छान्तिं निगच्छति |
कौन्तेय प्रतिजानीहि न मे भक्तः प्रणश्यति ||
(He quickly becomes righteous and attains lasting peace. O son of Kunti, declare it boldly that My devotee never perishes.)

I understand the infinite glory of ॐ (Om) as the crown jewel of all mantras, the center of spiritual success, and the source of all knowledge and creation. Chanting ॐ (Om) during life brings prosperity and detachment. But why is the chanting of ॐ (Om) at the moment of death so supremely important that it leads to the liberation of both the human body and the soul?

O Devi, the human body is called 'Brahmapura' (the city of Brahman). In the lotus of the human heart, the divine light of the soul shines. At the time of death, when a person chants the mantra ॐ (Om) with rhythm, both the individual soul and the Supreme Soul dance with great joy and bliss. They become so eager to unite, like two lovers separated for ages breaking all barriers to merge into each other.
Krishna, how should I decide what is right for me? What is my foremost duty, as no one else can truly make that decision for me?

Arjuna, the dharma of every being is individual. You yourself must decide what your primary duty is at that moment, because the voice of your soul is your dharma. This world is action-oriented. Therefore, abandoning all other duties, come to My refuge, as I have taught:सर्वधर्मान्परित्यज्य मामेकं शरणं व्रज।अहं त्वां सर्वपापेभ्यो मोक्षयिष्यामि मा शुचः॥(Abandon all varieties of dharma and simply surrender unto Me. I shall deliver you from all sinful reactions; do not fear.)

O Keshava, my heart is filled with anguish at the thought of fighting my own kin. How can I, driven by such deep emotions, bring myself to perform such a dreadful act? Are not these feelings, these relationships, the very foundation of action, the true motivators?

Arjuna, it is not emotion, but the knowledge of your duty (कर्तव्य का ज्ञान) that is required. One needs to understand their duty in a given situation. Emotions often obstruct the path of duty and weaken a person. Just as now, the attachment (मोह) born of your emotions is diverting you from your path of duty. Therefore, the scriptures declare that duty is higher than emotion. Your arguments, that there must be some inspiration for action, and that inspiration requires emotion, are all born of the attachment to your relationships (मोहजनित रिश्ते-नातों के मोह). This has clouded your intellect, and thus, you cannot see the truth.

But Keshava, you know that when a man performs any action, there is a cause, a motivator. Emotions are at the root of actions; it is for the fulfillment of these emotions that one performs good or bad deeds. Indeed, at the root of action lies emotion, and at the root of emotion lies a relationship. So, how can emotions arise without some connection, without some relationship?

Arjuna, you speak truly; indeed, relationships are the source from which the river of emotions flows. However, this river of emotions quickly dries up, just as drops of water disappear as they flow forward. Even before the pyre of the deceased turns cold, the tears in the eyes of relatives dry up. Some weep for a moment, some cry for a couple of days, but even a mother, after a few days, becomes entangled in the illusion of the world and returns to her other engagements. This world's ways are for four days, these relationships are for four days: चार दिनु की रीत जगत ने चार दिनों के नाते हैं. As soon as the eyes close, all relationships cease: पहले तुम के पर दुबे डे पड़ते ही सब नाते मिट जाते हैं. The four bearers carry the body from the house. Those for whom you fret, they light the pyre. Those on whose arms you rested, they immerse you in the river. Then, with a heavy heart, they sever their ties with you. By falling into the attachment of these fleeting relationships, people forget the true path and repeatedly return to the cycle of birth and death.
You stated earlier that true emotions arise from relationships. Yet, relationships often seem like a temporary display. How can I reconcile these two ideas, Keshava?

Indeed, Arjuna, I said that some emotion is necessary for action, and emotions often stem from relationships. However, if a person severs all ties and abandons their emotions, for whom will they act? Not for their Dharma. For Dharma, it is not emotion, but the knowledge of one's duty that is required. One must understand their duty in a given situation. Emotion can often obstruct the path of duty, weakening a person. For example, the attachment (मोह) born from your emotions right now is diverting you from your duty. Thus, the scriptures state that duty is superior to emotion. Your arguments, such as the need for inspiration and emotion for action, are all born of this very attachment. The attachment to relationships has clouded your intellect, preventing you from seeing the truth and clearly discerning Dharma at this moment.
Then what exactly is Dharma, Madhusudana? What is its order, and who determines its laws? Who are those who establish the principles of Dharma?

Arjuna, every individual makes the law of their own Dharma. Look, Partha, a Dharma whose law has been made by someone else cannot be truly yours. Your Dharma is that which you have formulated yourself, that which your own soul has accepted. Dharma is a personal matter, and one must decide it for oneself.
I still do not understand, Keshava.

Consider this, Partha, I will explain with an example. Imagine dacoits attacking a village and abducting its girls. At the same time, a man's father lies on his deathbed, taking his last breaths, repeatedly asking his son for a sip of water. What is that person's Dharma at that moment? Should he fulfill his filial duty by dropping drops of Ganga water into his dying father's throat in his final moments, or should he, as a protector of his village, pick up a sword to defend the girls in danger, confront the dacoits, and if necessary, sacrifice his life? How can anyone else decide this for him? This is called a Dharma-Sankat (धर्म-संकट), or a moral dilemma. In such a situation...
Keshav, I find myself deeply disturbed now, despite my efforts to uphold dharma.

O Arjuna, you were not swayed by worldly factors before, but why are you so troubled today? You did not forget your dharma then, but now you seem to be forgetting it. Would you like to know the reason?
Yes, Keshav.
Your mind is not under your control because you have not adopted Karma Yoga.
What did you say? Karma Yoga keeps the mind under control?

Yes, O Arjuna, due to Karma Yoga, the mind of a Karma Yogi does not wander. The intellect of a Karma Yogi becomes stable, just as strong rocks are not disturbed by the stormy waves of a river, nor can a great waterfall break a solid stone. Similarly, the mind of a Karma Yogi is not disturbed by external factors or emotions. Therefore, practice Nishkama Karma Yoga (action without desire for results). The greatest feature of Nishkama Karma Yoga is that you will not be bound by your actions, even while performing them.
O Keshav, how is this possible, that one can perform actions without being bound by karma? Tell me the way to perform actions and remain unbound.
The method is quite simple: do not be attached to the fruits of action.
But how can this be? Everyone desires the fruit of their actions!

O Arjuna, is it by mere wishing that a man attains results? No, for the fruit is in the hands of destiny (prarabdha). He who desires results gets distracted from his actions and duties by constantly thinking about the outcome, and thus often does not achieve the desired fruit. O Partha, man can only perform actions; the results are not in his control.

Keshav, if the attainment of results is not under the control of man's actions, then why should one act? It is man's dharma to perform his duties, and for this, action is necessary. But Keshav, if the desire for fruits is abandoned, how will the tendency to act arise in man? If there is no desire for fruit, why would anyone act?

O Arjuna, ordinary people who engage in action solely out of a desire for results get caught in the cycle of pleasure and pain, and their peace of mind is destroyed. Their minds are restless at every moment, constantly thinking about the attainment of results. Look at Duryodhana and his brothers; since childhood, Duryodhana, Shakuni, and Dushasana...

O Krishna, how is the cycle of karma connected to repeated births, such as those of Ravana, and how does it prevent the soul from attaining liberation (मोक्ष)? It seems that in one's life, the actions performed bear fruits of both sin (पाप) and merit (पुण्य). Sometimes there is more sin, sometimes more merit. Suffering through both, one performs new actions in a new life, and these are again tallied in the account of sin and merit. Thus, to experience these new karmas, one takes another new birth, and this cycle of birth after birth continues incessantly. How then can the soul unite with the Supreme Self, which is called liberation?

Indeed, Arjuna, you have well described the relentless cycle. The deeds a man performs in one life result in both good (पुण्य) and bad (पाप) consequences. These are tallied, and to experience their fruits, one takes on a new body. This chain of actions and reactions, leading to continuous rebirths, prevents the soul from merging with the divine, which is true liberation. As long as the ledger of sin and merit necessitates further experience, the soul remains bound to this material world.

Then, to attain liberation and escape the bondage of sin and merit, should a person renounce all actions and become a renunciant (संन्यासी)? Yet, no human can truly be inactive; one must perform actions in every situation. If so, why do renunciants abandon karma?

Hear me, Partha. Renunciants, too, do not, nor can they, abandon all actions. As I have said before, they also perform actions. Eating, drinking, sitting, rising, performing penance (तपस्या), and engaging in spiritual practices (साधना)—these are all actions. How can anyone escape their own actions? No man can be without action. The world functions only through action. As it is said, "कर्म किए दिन जगत में प्राणी मृतक समान" (A being without action is like a dead body in this world). If destiny (प्रारब्ध) alone dictates everything, why then perform actions? It is because karma forms one's destiny that the law of karma was established. If we were not entitled to action, then the fruits of actions would be immense. The attainment of the fruits of actions, Arjuna, is the account of births. Karma is the means to all dharma, hence the importance of karma is great. No one can be free from its cycle.
So, how then should we perform actions to achieve liberation from sin and merit?

Partha, the way is this: one should perform actions as one's duty, abandoning the desire for their fruits. Success will certainly come, but one should accept it as the will of providence. Wise men, adopting this very yoga, become Karma Yogis.

This is a profound truth, Lord! But how does this work, Bhagavan? All fear, worry, and suffering (क्लेश) arise from attachment (आसक्ति) to objects of desire (मोह). Karma Yoga, on the other hand, asks one to renounce attachment to the fruits of action, meaning to act without desire (निष्काम होकर कर्म करने को कहता है). What benefit does a person gain from this, O Lord?

My dear Arjuna, Karma Yoga purifies the intellect and makes one highly skilled and alert (चतुर शुद्ध और बहुत कर देता है). With a liberated and pure mind, one can lead a joyful life. Remember, Arjuna, when you went to attain celestial weapons (दिव्य अस्त्र) and gained the boon of Indra, you were not entangled in the enchanting illusion of Urvashi; you were not enchanted by her, because at that time your mind was unattached (निरासक्त). You have come here to dedicate yourself to the service of your guest, which is not unrighteousness; this is dharma.

Krishna, I recall the countless schemes the Kauravas devised to gain the throne. They even threw Bhima into the water, and then plotted to burn us all alive in the Lakshagraha. That plan was so cunning, it seemed impossible for us to escape alive! How could their meticulously planned actions repeatedly fail, and how could we survive such perilous situations despite their persistent malice?

Yes, Arjuna, you remember well. Those were indeed their heinous acts to secure the throne. But did their meticulously planned actions yield the fruit they desired? No, because the plan of प्रारब्ध (Prarabdha) was different. When all their attempts failed against the divine will, they resorted to deceit, sending you all into twelve years of exile and one year of incognito living. Yet, despite their repeated efforts, the Kauravas did not attain the results they wished for. They forgot that the fruit one receives is commensurate with their actions, not their desires. They are deeply entangled in the web of their misdeeds, Partha, and the fruit they covet will not be theirs. Instead, they will surely receive the bitter consequences of their evil actions. This truth, you must always remember.

O Krishna, you speak of a Sthitapragya, a man of steady wisdom. Does this mean one must stabilize the mind, preventing it from wavering, and always subordinate it to the intellect while performing actions? And how can one overcome these endless desires that grow unbound, from a mere hut to a royal palace?

Indeed, Arjuna. While controlling the mind and employing intellect is vital, relying solely on intellect can be perilous. In times of adversity or destruction, even a man's own intellect can become corrupted and lead him astray. The true path to peace and happiness lies in cultivating contentment within oneself, finding satisfaction in whatever state one is in. For the moment a being finds contentment, peace and happiness prevail.

But then, O Madhusudana, if one should neither act solely according to the mind's desires nor depend entirely on intellect, what then should a man do? How can one live against their inherent Pravritti (tendencies)? Please tell me, how can a person change their Pravritti to follow the path of liberation and salvation?

Before one can change their Pravritti, it is essential to understand how these tendencies are formed, Arjuna. From birth, a human being carries within them the three Gunas: Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas. This entire creation is formed based on these three qualities, and all beings possess them. However, in each being, one of these Gunas is more predominant, and this predominance shapes their character and desires. A person primarily influenced by Rajas yearns for opulence, grandeur, and dominion. A Tamasic person is lazy, negligent, and filled with negative emotions. Sattva is the purest of these qualities; a Sattvic person is honest and straightforward. Though all three Gunas are present in varying degrees in everyone, the dominant Guna determines one's Pravritti and inclinations. Thus, a person's desires arise from their innate tendencies and interests. One who is a Sthitapragya remains unattached to these worldly pulls, turning their focus away from the illusions of the material world, finding peace within and breaking free from all attachments, Arjuna.

O Madhusudana, if a person should neither act according to their own desires nor follow the advice of others, then what should they do? How can one live against their inherent nature (Pravritti), and how can a human being change their tendencies to adopt the path of liberation and salvation? Please tell me the way.

Before you can change your tendencies, O Partha, it is essential to understand how they are formed. Actions performed with faith in the Supreme, letting go of attachment to success and failure, are called Samattva Yoga, or equanimity in Yoga. Actions done with a spirit of surrender to God, without desiring their fruits, are far superior to those performed with an expectation of results. Wise individuals perform actions through Samattva Yoga, free from the need for outcomes, and thereby transcend the feelings of sin and merit. O Partha, you too will become free from such feelings when you practice Samattva Yoga.

योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि संगं त्यक्त्वा धनञ्जय।
सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते।।

O Dhananjaya, perform action, being steadfast in Yoga, abandoning attachment, and be even-minded in success and failure; for evenness of mind is called Yoga. This means maintaining stability whether in gain or loss, victory or defeat, honor or dishonor. Only then will your Yoga be perfected. Understand this, O Partha: a person who performs actions with a craving for results, even when doing noble deeds, cannot be a Karma Yogi. Such a person may achieve worldly benefits, but not the Supreme Self or true peace.
Krishna, for a human being, both sin and merit are binding. Through proper actions, one might be freed from sin, but how can one be freed from merit?

O Arjuna, feelings such as sin and merit, pleasure and pain, fame and infamy, are for ordinary human beings. However, true Karma Yogis are liberated from such dualities. They act by considering the voice of their inner self as the command of the Supreme. Where then is the question of sin or merit for them?

O Krishna, I understand how Karma Yogis transcend these dualities. But with my mind still clouded by delusion and attachment, how can I, who is currently overwhelmed by such thoughts, truly adopt this path of Nishkama Karma Yoga?

O Partha, if you are still under the sway of delusion, it will indeed be difficult. The darkness of delusion has cast a pall over your intellect. Remove it with the light of knowledge and pull your intellect out of the swamp of illusion.

यदा ते मोहकलिलं बुद्धिर्व्यतितरिष्यति।
तदा गन्तासि निर्वेदं श्रोतव्यस्य श्रुतस्य च।।

O Partha, when your intellect will cross the mire of delusion, then you will attain indifference to what has been heard and what is yet to be heard.
O Madhusudana, what does this *Sthitapragya* mean? Please explain it to me.

O Partha, a person whose mind is undisturbed amidst sorrow, who does not yearn for happiness, and whose heart has no place for afflictions like anger, delusion, and fear, is known as *Sthitapragya*. As it is said:
दुःखेष्वनुद्विग्नमनाः सुखेषु विगतस्पृहः।
वीतरागभयक्रोधः स्थितधीर्मुनिरुच्यते॥
O Krishna, how does such a *Sthitapragya* speak? How does he sit and how does he walk?

O Partha, a *Sthitapragya* attains spiritual peace in every state, be it joy or sorrow. Being absorbed in supreme bliss, such a person is never disturbed by sorrow or happiness. The mind of such a *Sthitapragya* is like a lamp in a windless place, whose flame remains steady and never flickers.

Lord Krishna, the common understanding of a Shiv Yogi's Yajna (यज्ञ) is to offer oblations into a fire pit. However, you say that any act for public welfare, or the sacrifice and renunciation of a dear object, is also Yajna. What is the true meaning of this?

Arjuna, it is true that beings, according to their own faith, perform havans and worship different deities in various ways; that is also called Yajna. Some people, without being indifferent, donate their wealth; that is also Yajna, called Dravya Yajna (द्रव्य यज्ञ). Some yogis selflessly impart knowledge; that is called Gyan Yajna (ज्ञान यज्ञ). In addition to this, there are also certain yogic practices of Ashtanga Yoga (अष्टांग योग) through which many yogis perform Yajna based on efforts for spiritual attainments for divine accomplishments.
Lord Krishna, you also speak of Ashtanga Yoga and Tantra. What is their explanation?

Arjuna, Ashtanga Yoga is a divine therapy of many kinds, by which all human diseases are destroyed, be they physical ailments, mental disorders, or spiritual knots. All means of treatment for these are described in Yoga Shastra. Among these, Pranayama (प्राणायाम), Mantra (मंत्र), and Tantra (तंत्र) are prominent.
How is this Yajna, which is based on Pranayama, performed?

O Arjuna, yogis, through both Mantra and Tantra methods, sometimes offer Prana Vayu (प्राण वायु) into Apana Vayu (अपान वायु), and sometimes Apana Vayu into Prana Vayu. And some yogi masters, through the knowledge of Yoga, stop the movement of both Prana Vayu and Apana Vayu, thus offering their Prana into Prana itself.
You have explained the various aspects of Yajna, but Lord, I wish to know more about Prana and Apana Vayu.

In Yoga, during Pranayama, the air that goes out is called Prana Vayu. And the breath that comes in is called Apana Vayu. Pranayama is also a Yajna, because in this Yajna, by offering Prana Vayu into Apana Vayu, a Pranayama called Pooraka (पूरक) happens. Conversely, by offering Apana Vayu into Prana Vayu, Rechaka (रेचक) Pranayama happens. In this way, through the control of both these, Pranayama is called Kumbhaka (कुम्भक). Besides these, there are other Vayus: Vyana (व्यान), Udana (उदान), and Samana (समान). The air that moves out of the body is called Vyana. And the air that distributes nutrients simultaneously to all parts of the body is called Samana.
Lord, you have mentioned Prana, Apana, Vyana, Samana, and Udana as the Pancha Pranas (पंचप्राण). Where are these located in the human body? Please explain their systematic arrangement to me.
Samana Vayu is located in the stomach.
For the welfare of humanity, which is the most superior form of sacrifice, O Krishna?

O Partha, Jnana Yagna (the sacrifice of knowledge) is far superior to Dravya Yagna (the sacrifice of material possessions). This is because the highest welfare of human beings can only be achieved through the power of knowledge. Knowledge alone enables humans to distinguish between good and bad, sin and virtue, dharma and adharma. Moreover, it is through knowledge that a living being attains the true understanding of God's form. Knowledge is a quality that purifies all faults, arrogance, and ego in human beings. Even the very root of devotion is knowledge.
What did you say? That devotion also originates from knowledge?

Yes, Arjuna.या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी।यस्यां जाग्रति भूतानि सा निशा पश्यतो मुनेः॥What is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled person is awake; and in that in which all beings are awake, that is night for the introspective sage.

O Keshava, if you are saying that Jnana Yoga (the path of knowledge) is superior to Karma Yoga (the path of action), then why are you instructing me to perform action and wage this war? Why are you inspiring me to commit destruction?

O Partha, I did not say that Jnana Yoga is superior to Karma Yoga. That was not the meaning of my words; you have been mistaken. O Partha, just as there might be two roads leading to a city, one from the north and another from the south, and though they come from different directions, they both lead to the same city; similarly, Jnana Yoga and Karma Yoga are two different means, but their ultimate goal is one. Through both paths, a seeker attains Brahman. Therefore, both Yogas are excellent. However, the practice of Sankhya Yoga, which is based on knowledge, is difficult. In comparison, the practice of Karma Yoga is easier. O sinless one, in this world, I have previously spoken of two types of devotion: for the Sankhyas (those pursuing knowledge), the path of Jnana Yoga; and for the Yogis (those pursuing action), the path of Karma Yoga.लोकेऽस्मिन् द्विविधा निष्ठा पुरा प्रोक्ता मयानघ।ज्ञानयोगेन सांख्यानां कर्मयोगेन योगिनाम्॥One does not attain freedom from action merely by abstaining from actions, nor does one achieve perfection by mere renunciation.

Lord, you are saying that whether it is the path of renunciation (Sannyasa Yoga) or the path of action (Karma Yoga), a being cannot escape action in either situation. Then how can a yogi attain the state of non-action (निष्कर्मता)?
A being can attain the state of non-action by performing all its actions without attachment, offering them to Me, the Supreme Lord.
O Krishna, what is meant by 'Nishkarmata,' and how can one achieve a state where actions do not produce karmic fruits?

O Arjuna, when a being dedicates all their actions to the Lord, no fruits are produced from such actions. In this way, by surrendering all actions to God and becoming absorbed in Him, one attains a state of oneness with the Absolute, known as Nishkarmata. Indeed, no one can remain without action, for all beings are compelled to act every moment by the Gunas born of Prakriti. Therefore, for one who is compelled to act, it is essential to perform actions as a sacrifice (Yajna). This Yajna, O Partha, is performed both for the welfare of the world and for the worship of the Lord. When you perform actions, dedicate them either for public welfare or as an offering to Me. This will make your actions pure, beneficial, and consecrated, like a sacrifice. By understanding action as Yajna, you will remain free from karmic bondage. For, O Partha, except for actions performed as Yajna, all other actions bind a person to this world. As it is said: यज्ञार्थात्कर्मणोऽन्यत्र लोकोऽयं कर्मबन्धनः। तदर्थं कर्म कौन्तेय मुक्तसङ्गः समाचर॥ (The world is bound by actions other than those performed for the sake of sacrifice; therefore, O son of Kunti, perform action for that sake, free from attachment.) When a person dedicates their body, mind, wealth, life, and all to the Supreme Soul, and performing welfare work, sees the Divine in every living being, this is what the Lord does.
Yes, Madhusudana, you speak of many types of Yajnas. Please describe their various forms in detail.

Partha, first understand what Yajna truly is. It is the act of dedicating one's best possessions, one's wealth, one's specific feelings, and even one's intense desires at My feet, the Supreme Self. The fundamental essence of Yajna is the sacrifice of what is dear to oneself. The scriptures state that a person who partakes of the remnants of a Yajna offering becomes free from all sins. However, those who cook food solely for their own sustenance, driven by selfish desires, verily partake of sin. Remember, O Arjuna, the scriptures describe many kinds of Yajnas through which beings worship and please the gods. But all these deities are indeed My forms; therefore, through these Yajnas, beings are essentially worshipping Me.
O Krishna, what are the benefits of performing the sacrifice in the form of Pranayama, as described in Yoga Shastra? How does one achieve spiritual consciousness through it?

Arjuna, by performing the sacrifice of Pranayama, a person gains strength to undertake benevolent actions for the welfare of the world. It bestows physical and mental health, leading to spiritual awakening. However, it is essential to first receive complete instruction from an accomplished Guru before attempting such a practice. One should humbly and repeatedly pray to the Guru, and a pleased Guru will impart all this knowledge. Proceeding on this path without a Guru's guidance can be very perilous.

O Madhusudan, you have described excellent virtues. However, some sacrifices cannot be performed by everyone; for instance, a poor person cannot perform a material sacrifice. Therefore, Krishna, for the welfare of humanity, please tell me, which is the most supreme sacrifice?

Partha, the sacrifice of knowledge is far superior to the sacrifice of material possessions, for the supreme welfare of humanity can only be achieved through the power of knowledge. Knowledge enables one to discern good from bad, and righteousness from unrighteousness. Indeed, through knowledge alone does a being truly understand the nature of God. Knowledge is like a fire where all the impurities of human beings—such as arrogance and ego—are consumed. Moreover, even the origin of devotion lies in knowledge. Arjuna, by reaching the peak of the mountain of knowledge, one realizes that high above this peak is a pure, clear sky where devotion reigns. When a being reaches this sky of devotion, the Lord Himself takes their hand and leads them to His divine feet. Understand this, Arjuna, that by climbing the final step of the ladder of knowledge, a being obtains the wings of faith (Shraddha). With the help of these wings of faith, the being begins to soar in the sky of devotion. This is why I have declared the sacrifice of knowledge to be the best. Partha, through knowledge, you will first see the entire creation within yourself, and then you will see yourself merged within that Supreme Being. When you attain knowledge, even if you are the greatest sinner in the world, you will easily cross the ocean of sin by sitting in the boat of this knowledge and reach the refuge of the Supreme Being.
O Krishna, caught in the complexities of duty and the quest for true liberation, I seek your ultimate counsel. What is the supreme path to attain inner peace and self-realization?

Arjuna, abandon all varieties of duties and simply surrender unto Me. I shall deliver you from all sinful reactions; do not fear.सर्वधर्मान्परित्यज्य मामेकं शरणं व्रज।अहं त्वा सर्वपापेभ्यो मोक्षयिष्यामि मा शुचः॥(Bhagavad Gita 18.66)Come under My shelter, for that continuous stream of devotion (भक्तिधारा) will forever flow, leading to self-realization (आत्मानुभव) for the entire world. I am indeed the ever-present Lord and your ultimate guide.

O Krishna, you speak of actions, saying that based on one's intention, the same deed can become either a sin or a virtuous act. You also mention that through knowledge, one can discern between Karma, Akarma, and Vikarma. What exactly are these — Karma, Akarma, and Vikarma?

Listen, O Partha. It is through the knowledge of the Self that one can identify Karma, Akarma, and Vikarma. Akarma refers to actions performed with a selfless attitude, without attachment to their results. Because one is not bound by the fruits of such actions, they are considered Akarmic. Karma, on the other hand, refers to actions performed with a desire for their fruits, and their results, good or bad, are inevitable according to Dharma. Vikarma encompasses unrighteous, improper, and forbidden deeds, such as dishonesty, deceit, and treachery. Just as the rising sun dispels the darkness of night, the light of knowledge destroys the darkness of ignorance, guiding a person on the path to the Supreme and preventing them from straying.
I understand the definitions, O Keshava. But how can the *same* action be both a sin and a virtuous act, depending on the intention? Could you illustrate this with an example?

Indeed, Partha, this is a crucial point. Let us take the example of killing another person. If a man murders another weak individual out of malice or personal gain, that act is undoubtedly a grave sin. However, consider a situation where a wicked person is attempting to assault an innocent woman, and to protect her, one kills the aggressor. In such a case, the act of killing, driven by the intention to defend the helpless, becomes a virtuous deed. It is clear that protecting the defenseless is an act of merit. You have, in essence, answered your own question. The underlying *bhava*, the intention or feeling with which an action is performed, is what determines whether the very same act becomes a sin or a virtuous deed.
O Keshav, if war is considered valor, where then is the humanity in it? What is the purpose of this battle that involves such destruction?

O Partha, you are still wandering in the darkness of ignorance, which is why you speak thus. Understand that when action is performed with the intention of destroying all sins, even if one falls in that war, the being attains heaven. Therefore, abandon all doubts and fight. When you attain true knowledge, you will understand that this entire world is My Maya. It originated from Me, I am its sustainer, and I am also its destroyer. Indeed, this creation is but a play of Maya.
If this world is Your Maya, what then is its true form or nature? How does this cosmic illusion manifest?

O Arjuna, if you perceive this with the eyes of knowledge, you will realize that the world of Maya is like a tall, inverted tree. Its roots are above, and its branches and leaves extend downwards. See it with your inner vision. As I said, this world of Maya originated from Me, hence its roots are above, representing Me, and the world of Maya is below, making the tree inverted. They speak of the imperishable Ashvattha (Pipal tree), whose roots are above and branches below, and whose leaves are the Vedic hymns; he who knows it is a knower of the Vedas:

ऊर्ध्वमूलमधःशाखमश्वत्थं प्राहुरव्ययम्।
छन्दांसि यस्य पर्णानि यस्तं वेद स वेदवित्॥

O Partha, being the expander of this world, Brahma is considered the main branch of this tree, and the Vedas are its leaves. The five sense objects—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—are like the categories of the tree's branches. This tree of Maya is continuously nourished by the qualities of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas (goodness, passion, and ignorance). A person trapped by attachments remains entangled in the branches of this tree. This tree is imperishable, a symbol of the darkness and Maya of the world.
O Madhusudana, if this creation is eternal and so vast, its immense shadow must be spread everywhere. How then can any human escape its pervasive influence and shadow?

O Arjuna, while it is true that this tree is vast, its creator is infinitely vaster. If you cut down this world-tree with the sword of knowledge and detachment, you will then attain the vision of that omnipresent, all-pervading Paramatma, who is everywhere. Therefore, Partha, devote yourself to Me.

I have no concern for material gain, but how can I commit the sin of slaying my own kinsmen? Even if they, deluded by greed, cannot see the grievous fault in destroying their family and the sin involved, we who can clearly perceive the ruin and the faults arising from this war must consider it. You know that the destruction of the family leads to the loss of eternal family traditions. When dharma is destroyed, the entire family becomes steeped in adharma, just as a deadly disease spreads through the body. Due to the spread of this sin, the women of the family become corrupt, and from their corruption, mixed progeny (Varna-sankara) arises. And because of the sin of Varna-sankara, the entire family line is condemned, and their ancestors also fall from their rightful place.कुलक्षये प्रणश्यन्ति कुलधर्माः सनातनाः |धर्मे नष्टे कुलं कृत्स्नमधर्मोऽभिभवत्युत ||अधर्माभिभवात् कृष्ण प्रदुष्यन्ति कुलस्त्रियः |स्त्रीषु दृष्टासु वार्ष्णेय जायते वर्णसंकरः || (Bhagavad Gita 1.39-40)How can I fight in such a battle? How can I commit the sin of destroying my own family with my own hands? I will not fight, I will never fight! It would be far better for me to take a begging bowl and wander from door to door, begging for alms. What a beautiful thought! I will not fight; I will beg for alms.

O Arjuna, such words are spoken not by a hero, but by a coward! You came to this battlefield to demonstrate your valor! For this, you acquired the Pashupatastra from Lord Shiva, and after years of intense penance, you obtained divine weapons from your father, Indra! Do you not remember your mother Kunti's final message: 'Whenever you return to my presence, return victorious, with the mark of victory, made from the blood of the Kauravas, on your forehead!' O Arjuna, remember, the responsibility to fulfill your mother's vow rests upon you. Therefore, cast off this petty weakness of heart and fight like a Kshatriya! It is the duty of a Kshatriya to fight!

O Madhusudana, I too know that I am a Kshatriya, and fighting is my dharma. But seeing these kinsmen eager for battle on this battlefield, my body trembles, my heart falters, and my mouth is parched. My mind is bewildered by conflicting thoughts. Due to this confusion, my path is unclear. O Krishna, You are my Guru, and I have taken refuge in You. Please guide me and show me what is definitively good for me.
O Krishna, what truly happens to one who dies? Does everything truly perish with the body? I am bewildered by this cycle of birth and death, and the sorrow it brings.

That which is born is certain to die, and that which dies is certain to be reborn. For only the body is destroyed, not the soul within it, which never perishes. Understand, O Partha, there are but two entities in this world: the body, and the soul residing within it. The soul, which resides within the body, never dies. But the body is impermanent. The soul merely sheds one body and acquires another, just as a person discards old clothes and puts on new ones.वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय नवानि गृह्णाति नरोपराणि ।तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णा न्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही ॥It is simply a change of attire, a transformation. Consider death and birth as two doors facing each other. When a being arrives at the door of death, that body perishes, and the light of the soul leaves it, moving forward to enter the door of birth. There, the soul receives a new body, and a new journey of birth begins. O Partha, the soul is eternal and therefore does not change, but the body is perishable, so the same soul changes many bodies across different births. Thus, in every new birth, it continues to assume new bodies.
My Lord, I do not understand this concept. How can an individual receive many bodies within a single lifetime? Surely, a being receives only one body in one birth, does it not?

No, not just one; many bodies are received even within a single lifetime. I shall explain. Recall your own childhood, Arjuna. What was your body like then? You were a tiny infant. And where is that body now? That body has changed. Your current body is not the same; today, you have the body of a young man. Similarly, at birth, a being receives the body of an infant, which, under the influence of time, becomes the body of a child, then, in adolescence, it becomes the body of a youth, and finally, the body of an aged person. It is like a withered leaf detaching from the tree of life. Thus, this body, which is constantly moving towards its destruction moment by moment, should not be a cause for your grief. For this reason, the scriptures declare: कृष्णं वन्दे जगद्गुरुम्
O Krishna, I wish to observe the Kaurava army. Please take my chariot to the middle of the two armies. I want to see who has assembled to make Duryodhana victorious, and against whom I must fight.

O Arjuna, as per your wish, I have brought your chariot here, between the two armies. Behold the enemy's army! Standing at the forefront are Bhishma, your great-grandfather and a formidable adversary to the Pandavas, and your guru, Dronacharya. To their left is Prince Duryodhana. If you wish for the Pandavas to be victorious, you must fight them all.

No, I cannot become an instrument of such bloodshed! My very soul trembles at the thought. How can I possibly harm my own kinsmen, my revered elders? For a disciple, a guru is like a father, like God. How can I disrespect them? How can I use the very knowledge of archery they imparted to me to shower arrows upon them, to pierce their hearts? Only a fallen, debased person could do such a thing! Bhishma, my grandfather, is not just venerable but truly worshipful. I cannot even raise my eyes to him, how can I raise weapons against him? O Krishna, when my feet had not yet learned to walk, Bhishma held my hand and taught me every step on the path of life. From his heart, rivers of love have always flowed for me. How can I then pierce his heart with a sword, and cause rivers of blood to flow?

O Partha, no weapon can cut the soul, no fire can burn it, no water can wet it, nor can the wind dry it. नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः। न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुतः॥ Understanding this, you should neither grieve for anyone's death nor rejoice in it. The soul is eternal, unborn, and imperishable.

O Krishna, my heart is filled with sorrow and confusion. How can I fight against my own kinsmen, my gurus, and my elders? I see no good in this war; it seems only to lead to sin and destruction. I feel weak and uncertain of my duty.

Do not succumb to the ocean of emotions; learn to master your mind. Do not destroy your glory by displaying weakness, O valiant one. For a warrior, the destruction of his glory is akin to death. Therefore, fight! Protect your honor, your duty, and your dharma. Even if you are slain in this righteous war, you will attain the abode of heroes and become immortal. People will forever recount your ignominy; for a respectable man, dishonor is worse than death. अकीर्तिं चापि भूतानि कथयिष्यन्ति तेऽव्ययाम्। संभावितस्य चाकीर्तिर्मरणादतिरिच्यते॥ Therefore, rise, O son of Kunti, and resolve to fight! Either slain, you will attain heaven, or conquering, you will enjoy the earth. Therefore, arise, O son of Kunti, determined to fight. हतो वा प्राप्स्यसि स्वर्गं जित्वा वा भोक्ष्यसे महीम्। तस्मादुत्तिष्ठ कौन्तेय युद्धाय कृतनिश्चयः॥
O Vasudeva, you know that I do not fear my own death even a bit.

Indeed, I know, O Dhananjaya, that you do not flinch from sacrificing your life in this righteous war. Your heart's weakness stems only from your attachments to your relatives, which are meaningless in the field of dharma. You are concerned about the death of your relations, but this thought is a clear symbol of your delusion.

You speak correctly, Keshava. At this moment, my intellect is steeped in the darkness of ignorance. I have lost the knowledge of what is dharma and what is adharma. I stand at such a crossroads of action where I cannot discern the path of righteousness from the path of unrighteousness. Show me the way to emerge from this darkness of ignorance, Keshava! Show me the way!

No, Partha! I wish to lead you out of this very darkness of ignorance. Instead of flailing blindly in this gloom, give direction to your foresight and look towards this creation! In this creation, whoever is born is surely subject to death. This means that every being in this mortal world, be it human, animal, bird, or plant—every living creature—brings its death along with its birth. Every being must die, that is, abandon its body, at a destined time. Therefore, leaving aside the worry of their deaths, understand your duty and fight! For to one that is born, death is certain, and to one that dies, birth is certain. Therefore, you should not grieve over the unavoidable. जातस्य हि ध्रुवो मृत्युर्ध्रुवं जन्म मृतस्य च। तस्मादपरिहार्येऽर्थे न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि॥
But Krishna, it is written in the scriptures that if the time for Grandfather Bhishma's death has come, he will surely depart. But why should I be the one to kill him with my own hands?
Do you truly wish to slay your own Bhishma Pitamah with your hands? Is this the truth?
No, I cannot bring myself to kill Grandfather Bhishma with my own hands.

Then tell me, who is this 'your Bhishma Pitamah' you are concerned about? Why do you ask this? Can you not see him? Is he not standing there, Grandfather Bhishma, on that chariot? The very one whom you see on the chariot, Partha!

O Jagatguru, just as our bodies, akin to a shell, are known to follow their nature: they are born as children, grow into youth, then youth begins to fade, leading to old age. When the soul leaves that aged body, the body dies. But where does the soul go then? Where and how does the soul reside without a body?

O Arjuna, after leaving an old body, the soul dwells in a new one, entering a child's body as consciousness. Then the same cycle begins again: birth, growing up, learning to walk, stumbling, and various bodily acts. Understand this much, and you will neither grieve for anyone's death nor fear your own. Just as the embodied soul continuously passes from boyhood to youth to old age within this body, similarly the soul passes into another body at death. We are not these bodies; we are the souls residing within them. This body is merely our vehicle, and we are its masters. Just as a chariot breaking does not destroy the charioteer, similarly, the joys and sorrows of the body do not make the soul happy or sad.

देहिनोऽस्मिन् यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा।
तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति॥
If that is so, then why does our soul experience these joys and sorrows?

These experiences of joy and sorrow are not felt by the soul, but by the body. The soul experiences nothing of this sort because existence, non-existence, joy, sorrow, heat, and cold are all rules of nature. The soul, however, is an imperishable part of the Supreme, therefore it is beyond the limits of nature. The soul is inconceivable; it cannot be grasped by human consciousness. O Arjuna, the rules of nature and creation do not apply to the soul, for it is beyond the reach of both creation and nature. Just as a spark is a part of the fire, so too is the soul a part of the Supreme Being. Therefore, it is eternal, unborn, everlasting, all-pervading, steady, and immutable.

अच्छेद्योऽयमदाह्योऽयमक्लेद्योऽशोष्य एव च।
नित्यः सर्वगतः स्थाणुरचलोऽयं सनातनः॥

Neither do weapons cut this soul, nor does fire burn it; water does not wet it, nor does the wind dry it.

नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः।
न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुतः॥
O Keshav, even after knowing all this – that the soul is eternal, unchanging, and unborn – why then do I lament or feel sorrow for the passing of bodies?
O Arjuna, understanding all this, you should neither mourn anyone's death nor exhibit joy over anyone's non-death.

Lord Krishna, Bhishma Pitamah is just a body. Who then is the real Bhishma Pitamah? Where is he? I don't understand your words. I see this body, but it is not Bhishma Pitamah. If this is just a body, then who is the real Bhishma Pitamah?

Listen attentively, Arjuna. I will explain. That which is light within the body, which is called the Atma (soul), that is the real Bhishma Pitamah. I grant you divine vision so you may see with these divine eyes that the Atma, the light within the body, is indeed the true Bhishma Pitamah.
Yes, Krishna, that is very good. I begin to understand.

Now, behold! If I were to sever Bhishma Pitamah's body with my Sudarshan Chakra, only his body would perish, but the light of his Atma would not be extinguished. See, I shall make this vision come alive for your divine eyes. You see, Arjuna, my Sudarshan Chakra has only destroyed the body, but the lamp of his Atma continues to burn just as brightly. Understand this ultimate truth well: in this world, only the body is perishable, but the Atma is imperishable. Upon the death of the body, the Atma does not die. The Atma is neither born nor does it ever die; it is unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient. It is not slain when the body is slain. Consider this: न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे

Lord, your words are confusing my intellect! You are saying two things at once that seem contradictory. You say the body dies, but a part of the body, which you call the Atma, does not die. How can a part of something remain when the whole perishes?

No, Arjuna, I did not say the Atma is a 'part' of the body. I said that the Atma and the body are two separate entities. Just as you and your armor are two separate things—if your armor is broken into pieces, it does not mean that Arjuna has been broken into pieces. Similarly, just as you and your chariot are two separate things, so too are a person's body and their Atma two separate entities. Understand that the chariot in which Arjuna sits is not Arjuna; Arjuna is the one sitting in the chariot, the charioteer.
But Krishna, even if the soul is separate, if my body perishes, won't there still be sorrow and grief?

Arjuna, hearing your words, I find myself amused by your intellect! On your own, you speak lofty words like a great scholar and a wise man. But you do not know that truly wise people do not grieve for those who have died, nor for those who are still alive. This is because they understand that one who has died will be born again, and one who is now alive...
How can I possibly shed the blood of my own kinsmen? I cannot bring myself to commit such an act, Krishna. It feels inherently wrong to fight against those I hold dear.

O Arjuna, the words you utter now, standing amidst this battlefield, are not befitting a true warrior. Your tongue tirelessly declares them 'your own,' flowing with rivers of love, affection, and drama in your mind. But remember, these very people silently witnessed the spectacle of your wife Draupadi being disrobed thirteen years ago in the assembly. Not a single one of them raised a hand to protect her. And those same hands are now raised to kill you! In their grasp, arrows thirst for the blood of you and the Pandavas. Are these truly 'your own' for whom you now speak words of love and respect?
But even so, they are my relatives, my family. It is difficult to see them only as adversaries. Who, then, are my true 'own' in this fight if not them?

You stand not in a wedding pavilion, Arjuna, but on a battlefield. Those whom you imagine as 'your own' have not come here to welcome or honor you; they have come with your and your brothers' names inscribed on their weapons. In their eyes, you will see a fierce thirst for the death of the Pandavas. These are your enemies, not your kinsmen in spirit. Your true 'own' are those who stand with you in life and death, shoulder to shoulder, ready to fight for your welfare. They are eager to hear the twang of your Gandiva bow right now! O Partha, your vision is clouded by attachment. Those you call 'your own' have not come to embrace you, but to play Holi with your blood. They know that to win this war, they must eliminate the mighty warrior named Arjuna. You hesitate to kill them because you consider them 'your own,' but if you do not strike them down, they will surely kill you and all of you.

My heart is filled with profound sorrow, O Krishna. How can I fight against my own kinsmen and revered teachers? I see no good in slaying them; rather, I would prefer to live by begging than to enjoy wealth stained with their blood. I am utterly confused, my mind bewildered by doubt. Please tell me definitively what is best for me, for I have taken refuge in You.

You speak great words of knowledge, yet you grieve for those who should not be grieved for. The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead. You speak words of wisdom, but your mind is filled with sorrow for what is inevitable.

अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे। गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिताः॥

O Partha, your knowledge is incomplete, and incomplete knowledge is like a double-edged sword that harms both the one who gives it and the one who receives it. You are doing the opposite of what is required; you hold the sword of incomplete knowledge, and you have abandoned your Gandiva.

O Keshav, what should I do? My mind and intellect are wavering like the pans of a balance scale of dharma, with equal measures of wisdom and ignorance. I find myself standing at a crossroads. I have come to You for refuge; please show me the true path, the real way forward.

O Arjuna, at this moment, you are not only standing on the dividing line of this battlefield, but your intellect is also poised between life and death. You are trying to escape your duty and your dharma. However, turning away from your duty or becoming distracted from this war will not change the law of destiny, for the will of the creator is firm and infallible. What makes you think that if you do not slay them, they will not die? No, Arjuna, even if you do not kill them, they will die, for the time of their death has already been predetermined in their destiny. According to this law, I have already slain them. You are merely an instrument through whom I wish to accomplish their demise. So, either perform your duty, or destiny will compel you to act.
What should I do, Madhusudana? How can I control my mind? How can I crush my own emotions beneath my feet? Tell me, Madhusudana, what should I do?
O Partha, abandon those emotions that deter you from the path of Dharma.
O Keshav, if fire cannot burn the soul, and weapons cannot cleave it, then why does the soul of a living being experience the pain of sorrow, happiness, honor, dishonor, and the pleasure of joy?
Partha, I have already told you that the experience of pleasure and pain is the work of the body, not the soul.

But Keshav, the body only feels pain when it is physically harmed, such as when one is injured or falls. That is physical pain. However, when there is dishonor, sorrow arises, and when there is honor, joy comes. In these instances, the body is not physically hurt. So, aren't the pain of dishonor and the suffering of disrepute felt by the soul itself?
No, Arjuna. Honor, dishonor, gain, loss, victory, defeat, pleasure, or pain – these are not experienced by the soul either. This is not the work of the soul; this is merely the mischief of the mind.
The mischief of the mind? What does that mean, Keshav?

Partha, the mind is an invisible organ of the living being's body, unseen yet it is the most powerful part of the body. Remember that the mind is a part of the body; it has no connection with the soul. If the soul is the master seated in the chariot, then the mind is the charioteer of the chariot-like body. It is this mind that drives the horses of the senses astray. Sometimes, in the fervor of its own power, this restless mind deludes a person into believing they are omnipotent, that they can do anything, that they are the king of the world before whom everyone is compelled to bow and whom everyone adores. Just as the wick of a lamp does not see the darkness hidden behind the lamp itself, similarly, youth does not see old age and weakness hidden behind it. But when the oil of youth's energy in the lamp of the body begins to burn out, and the darkness hidden within the lamp becomes apparent, then the mind starts to cry out in panic, 'I am sick!' This fear of illness and death is also caused by the mind. Arjuna, it is only the mind, that hypocrite, which intoxicates a person with the wine of 'I' and ego, making them delirious. Understand this, that the non-existent never comes into being, and the existent never ceases to be. The seers of truth have realized the nature of both: नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः। उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः॥ Therefore, make this mind your servant. Control this mind, and do not let it control you. When a person completely withdraws their senses from sense objects, just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs into its shell, then their wisdom becomes firmly established: यदा संहरते चायं कूर्मोऽङ्गानीव सर्वशः। इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता॥

O Beloved of devotees, O devotee of devotees, O God of gods, O Lord of Yoga, O Master of the universe, I, an ignorant one, a partaker of sin, have been granted divine knowledge by your grace. You have led me from the darkness of ignorance to the light of knowledge, and for this, I am deeply grateful. So grateful that even if I were to bow my head at your lotus feet for millions of years, and shed tears to fill hundreds of vast oceans, I still could not repay this kindness. For this supremely confidential and spiritual gift of knowledge, I offer you countless thanks. Before your supreme knowledge, I bow my head, and with my corrupted intellect, my every desire, my every hope, and my every longing, I dedicate myself, my body, and my mind to you. All this was a gift of your mercy, which I place at your holy feet. And in my ignorance, having considered you merely a human, my friend and companion, I may have inadvertently made mistakes or hurt your sentiments. Forgive me for that, O Ocean of Mercy, and accept my humble surrender, granting me your grace.
O Arjuna, behold these tears! In this river of tears, you have washed away every mistake and every sin. You are now sinless. Your wisdom has lifted the burden of sins from your soul.

Yes, my Lord, in the divine fire of your knowledge, my mind, my intellect, my being, and my ego—everything has turned to ashes. All burdens have been lifted from my soul. I feel as if an ant, sitting on a leaf, crosses a stormy river. In the same way, sitting upon the lotus leaf of your compassion, I am floating above this vast ocean of existence. Just as at the end, a dead body separates from the soul, similarly, at this moment, all my attachments, all my hopes, all my desires have departed from me, and I have become light like a ray of light. Now, it feels as if there is no burden on my entire existence; there is only light, light all around.
Blessed art thou, Arjuna.

O Madhusudan, you say that man remains caught in the delusion of Maya until his last breath, and thus becomes entangled in the cycle of birth. But you yourself created this world of Maya and, on the other hand, endowed humans with a restless mind, entangling both with each other. At every step, countless attractions are created to lead man astray. Man remains caught in this trap, and forgive me, but it seems you, like a hunter, watch the trapped man struggle and squirm, as if enjoying a spectacle.
No, Arjuna, I do not watch a spectacle. Rather, I observe the divine play (leela) of My Maya.

Yet, you merely observe, don't you? You don't offer help when a poor creature is wandering here and there, having lost its way. Does the thought of helping that unfortunate human never cross your mind? To step forward, hold his hand, and show him the true path?
Indeed it does, and I do help humanity.

But when? When do you help them? I see that you have created the law of Karma, set the cycle of birth and death in motion, and ensnared man in this whirlpool. This is no help at all! This is no assistance!

I certainly provide assistance. I never abandon My devotee. But if man would look towards Me, if he would move towards Me for help, then I would help him, would I not? However, instead of turning towards Me, he remains steeped in his ego, caught in the pride of his own strength. He remains under the illusion that there is no one greater than him in this world. He relies only on his intellect and his own might. He trusts his physical strength more than his own God.

To help a man who has strayed from his path, what is it that you ultimately desire from him? Do you want offerings of gold and silver? Do you wish for delicious and elaborate meals from your devotees?

I desire nothing from man but faith (shraddha). I ask for nothing else. He need not offer me lavish offerings. Gold, silver, ghee, sandalwood, and elaborate meals are not what I seek. With faith and devotion, be it a fruit, a flower, a single leaf, a drop of water, or even half a grain of rice – I accept it with far greater devotion than the devotee offers it. As it is said: पत्रं पुष्पं फलं तोयं यो मे भक्त्या प्रयच्छति। तदहं भक्त्युपहृतमश्नामि प्रयतात्मनः॥ (Bhagavad Gita 9.26)

O Lord, what is this boundless, infinitely effulgent, and eternal form that I behold before me? I am utterly overwhelmed with both wonder and intense fear. Never have I witnessed such a magnificent and awe-inspiring sight. Why have you revealed this extraordinary vision to me?

By the power of My Yoga, I have manifested to you this supreme, effulgent, beginningless, and endless form. This boundless cosmic vision, O son of Pandu, has never been shown by Me to anyone before. It is solely out of My profound affection for you that I have granted you the sight of this form. You should not be distressed by it. Behold, I am the great Destroyer, Mahakal, who annihilates all worlds. In My mouth, thousands of creations are dissolved every moment, and from My mouth, millions of universes constantly emerge. This entire creation, comprised of countless stars and millions of suns, is merely a play of My will. When I desire, I create them; when I desire, I destroy them. I am both life and death. Remember, O Arjuna, I am the origin, the middle, and also the end of all beings. अहमादिश्च मध्यं च भूतानामन्त एव च ॥

My Lord, I see countless eyes, mouths, and vast bellies, and Your terrifying jaws are ablaze with fire, into which hordes of all beings are rushing. My heart trembles with fear at this dreadful vision. I see wicked and evil-doers entering Your fierce mouths. What is the purpose of this terrible destruction, and how can I truly comprehend Your unfathomable vastness and this terrifying aspect?

O devotee, the cosmic form I have assumed now, accepting your prayers due to your immense devotion, is complete for your understanding alone. You cannot comprehend My existence with your intellect, nor can you fully perceive My complete form with divine sight alone. All your worldly imaginations will fail to grasp My entire existence. However, only through pure devotion can you truly feel the immensity of My boundless vastness – only a glimpse of it. The numerous eyes, faces, and formidable teeth you perceive are aspects of My universal form, which takes infinite shapes. Indeed, many evil-doers are entering My fiery mouths; this vision reveals the inevitable end of the wicked and the necessary re-establishment of Dharma. I am the eternal protector of the world and Mahakal; whenever Dharma is in peril, I manifest with My divine weapons to uphold righteousness. Therefore, O Arjuna, abandon all fear and agitation, and simply hold this form in your heart with unwavering faith and devotion. Merely remember My name: जय श्री कृष्ण (Jai Shri Krishna), केशव नमः (Keshava Namah), माधव नमः (Madhava Namah). Only through such devotion can you truly understand and absorb My infinite nature. दीयते यस्मै दिव्यदृष्टिस्तस्यैव दिव्यदर्शनम् ॥

O Mahakal, O Mahakaya, I see blazing flames consuming all like fuel. The wicked are perishing, yet even my own dear ones are being annihilated before my very eyes! The universe is terrified, mountains are shaken, directions are confused, and even the most patient have lost their composure before you, the Virat Swaroop, who seems to envelop everything. Who are you in this fearsome form, and what is your purpose?

Indeed, I am Time, the mighty destroyer of worlds, manifested here to annihilate all beings. Even without your action, none of the warriors assembled here will survive. I am the one who guides the twelve Adityas, eleven Rudras, and eight Vasus; who governs the Gandharvas, Dikpatis, Yakshas, and Nagapatis. I am the giver of good or bad destinies according to their actions, the bestower of welfare and liberation, the Supreme Lord who extends beyond all limits, yet can dwell within the hearts of my devotees. Therefore, cast aside all other duties and surrender completely unto Me. I shall liberate you from all sinful reactions; do not fear.
सर्वधर्मान्परित्यज्य मामेकं शरणं व्रज।
अहं त्वा सर्वपापेभ्यो मोक्षयिष्यामि मा शुचः॥
O Madhusudana, what kind of devotion or offerings are truly dear to you, that you accept with such grace?

Arjuna, I do not seek opulent offerings of gold, silver, ghee, sandalwood, or elaborate dishes. With true faith and devotion, even a simple fruit, a flower, a leaf, a drop of water, or even half a grain of rice is enough. I accept it with far greater devotion than the devotee's own, for:
पत्रं पुष्पं फलं तोयं यो मे भक्त्या प्रयच्छति।
तदहं भक्त्युपहृतमश्नामि प्रयतात्मनः॥
If even that is not possible, a single tear of faith or devotion is enough. I accept even that. My entire existence is permeated by that tear of devotion. A tear of devotion or repentance, even if shed in the last moments after countless sins, I accept that unparalleled offering. I wash away all the sins of that person with that tear, making them as pure as a newborn, ensuring their well-being, and granting them liberation.
Lord, if offering just a fruit, flower, or leaf grants liberation, then what becomes of karma, vikarma, sin, merit, dharma, and scriptural injunctions? Do they all become insignificant?

These dharmas, injunctions, and all their principles are like the moon and countless stars that glimmer in the darkness of adharma and ignorance. But when the sun of devotion rises, all these disappear. As long as the veil of 'I' and 'mine' remains, I am not seen. One whose heart has not called out to Me has not received My grace. I am fond of the sentiment of surrender; I meet those who call Me from their heart, saying, 'Hey Nath Narayana Vasudeva!' This means the place of devotion is so exalted that even dharma becomes trivial before it. However, this must be devotion free from attachment.
You speak of devotion without attachment, one that doesn't require pundits, discourses, or elaborate puja materials. What then, Madhusudana, is this one essential condition for such devotion?

The condition is this: with complete faith and full devotion, surrender yourself and all your actions to Me. That is all. I abandon everything else for such a devotee and grant them liberation, for:
सर्वधर्मान् परित्यज्य मामेकं शरणं व्रज।
अहं त्वां सर्वपापेभ्यो मोक्षयिष्यामि मा शुचः॥

Lord, you have indeed shown the path to liberation for all humanity. It is wonderful that you've revealed such a simple and accessible path of devotion. But then you say, "O Arjuna, the place of devotion is so high that I Myself worship My true devotees." What are you saying, Madhusudana? How can you, being the Supreme Lord, worship a devotee? If the Supreme Lord also becomes a devotee, then what difference remains between the two?
This is precisely the difference I wish to erase: the distinction between devotion, devotee, and God.

O Lord, although Your divine light has illuminated my inner being, I confess that I am not yet completely free from desires. Your radiance has not been able to consume all my longings; one desire still remains within me.
O Arjuna, what is this desire that even the brilliance of My light could not incinerate?

It is the desire for Your darshan (दर्शन), O Bhagavan. Not just this current form, but I wish to behold Your complete, universal form. I have heard explanations of Your various qualities and diverse forms in different incarnations. I long to see all those forms, all those qualities, simultaneously, at once! O Lord of all animate and inanimate beings, if You are pleased with me, please fulfill this ultimate wish.

O Pārtha, I have always called you My friend. I can indeed fulfill your wish, but your eyes will not be able to bear the splendor of My Cosmic Form (विराट स्वरूप). O Arjuna, your vision is not vast enough to encompass My complete divine form.

My eyes may be small, O Lord, but Your compassion and mercy are not! A true giver does not lessen his gift upon seeing a supplicant's small bag. Similarly, O Infinite One, grant me those eyes by which I may behold Your Cosmic Form (विराट रूप)!

O Arjuna, like a true devotee, today you have prevailed over God! It is well. I will certainly fulfill your wish. Today, because of you, all the demigods will also be blessed by witnessing this rare form of Mine. First, I bestow upon you the divine vision by which you can behold this Cosmic Form (विराट रूप).

O Great Cosmic Form (हे महा विराज स्वरूप)! O Fearsome Form (हे महा विकराल रूप)! O Supreme Lord! Seeing Your colossal figure, I am filled with astonishment and gripped by fear. From Svarga-loka to Pātāla-loka, only Your immense and terrifying form is visible! You are beyond the limits of my divine vision. Where Your existence begins and where it ends, I cannot comprehend. My intellect is bewildered. Please explain to me, who are You? Who are You? O Mighty-armed One (हे महा बाहू), Your fierce light is scorching the entire universe with its brilliance. Have mercy on me and tell me, who are You, who possess such a formidable form?
O Arjuna, showing you My grace (अनुग्रह) and revealing My supreme Yogic power...

O Krishna, you instruct on disciplining the mind, comparing it to a resolute rider mastering a horse through continuous effort. But even when the mind is brought to the right path by such practice, why is detachment still necessary? What prevents the mind from straying again, and how can one truly achieve lasting control?

Arjuna, indeed, with firm resolve, a rider eventually controls their horse, and similarly, through consistent practice (अभ्यास), one can bring their mind under control. However, even after the mind is set on the right path by the 'sword of practice', the 'sword of detachment (वैराग्य)' is indispensable. This is because the mind, once aligned, can still be pulled back to the wrong path by the pervasive allure of sensory objects, pleasures, and desires. Therefore, it is crucial for the mind to comprehend that all these worldly enjoyments are illusory, mere delusions born from Yogamaya. When the mind grasps this profound truth, it will no longer be attached to these subjects; rather, it will become truly detached (वैरागी). This is the function of the 'sword of detachment': to sever the bonds of attachment to sensory objects and transform the mind into that of a renunciant. Through this, you will cross the ocean of delusion, and your mind will be filled with dispassion towards all worldly and otherworldly pursuits. Your mind and body will become stable, and your soul will merge into the ocean of the Supreme Self.

Lord, I hear your words and understand that this entire world is transient, and true knowledge can indeed awaken detachment within one's heart. However, despite your profound wisdom, my mind struggles to fully accept and internalize this truth. Why is it so difficult for me to grasp it completely?

Arjuna, you find it difficult to accept that knowledge because you have not yet emerged from the darkness of delusion and attachment (मोह भ्रम). Therefore, you are presently unable to fully comprehend and embrace that wisdom. But do not despair. सर्वधर्मान्परित्यज्य मामेकं शरणं व्रज। अहं त्वां सर्वपापेभ्यो मोक्षयिष्यामि मा शुचः॥ Abandon all varieties of religion and just surrender unto Me. I shall deliver you from all sinful reactions; do not fear.
O Keshava, the mind is indeed restless! Just as it is impossible to control the blowing wind, similarly, it is extremely difficult to subdue this fickle mind.
O Arjuna, your statement is true; the mind is exceedingly restless, and it is very difficult to bring it under control. It is difficult, but not impossible.
Do you mean there is a way, a means to control the mind?

Certainly there is. O Arjuna, the hypocritical mind alone is that which intoxicates a person with the wine of egoistic pride. In its hands are attachment and illusion, which it uses to ensnare human desires, thereby keeping one in its control. This mind feels attachment to the body, to its joys, and to its sorrows. In joy, it sings songs of happiness, and in sorrow, it hums tunes of grief. It finds happiness in involving others in its suffering. This mind never allows any living being to escape its web until the very end of life, tying them with a rope and making them dance to its tunes. It gives no one a moment of leisure to look within themselves, recognize their soul (Atman), and realize the light of the Supreme Soul (Paramatman) that shines within the Atman. O Partha, it is therefore essential for a being to control their mind, look within themselves, and perceive the Atman. Then, within that Atman, the light of the Paramatman will clearly appear. This is what is called the realization of the Paramatman.

You say that one should look within to recognize the Atman and the Paramatman illuminated within the Atman. Then, is there someone else, distinct from the Atman, who recognizes the Atman? To whom are you saying this? Who will recognize the Atman? Is it the mind, which you say traps a being in the illusionary web of Maya and makes it dance? How can that mind then realize the Atman and Paramatman?

You have asked a good question, Arjuna. The answer is that as long as you allow yourself to remain under the sway of the mind and its thoughts, it will continue to make you dance to its tunes. O Partha, consider this body to be a chariot. The horses of this chariot are the human senses – understand them as the eyes, nose, ears, mouth, tongue, and fingers. The charioteer who guides these horses is the mind. And the one seated in that chariot, who is the master of this chariot, is the Atman. The human senses are naturally attracted towards their objects, and the mind often directs these senses towards their objects, pulling them along.

O Madhusudana, it is easy to declare that one should control the mind and become its master. Yet, this appears to be the most arduous task, O Keshava! The mind is as restless as the wind; just as it is impossible to control the blowing wind, it seems equally challenging to bring this fickle mind under control.

O Arjuna, your concern is valid. It is indeed true that the mind is exceedingly restless and challenging to subdue. However, O Janardana, it is difficult, but not impossible. It is certainly arduous, but not unachievable.
You say it is not impossible. Then, is there a specific method, a means by which this mind can be brought under control?

Indeed, there is. Listen, O mighty-armed (Arjuna):
असंशयं महाबाहो मनो दुर्निग्रहं चलम्।
अभ्यासेन तु कौंतेय वैराग्येण च गृह्यते।।
(Undoubtedly, O mighty-armed Arjuna, the mind is restless and difficult to curb. But by practice, O son of Kunti, and by dispassion, it can be controlled.)
To conquer the mind, one must wield two 'swords': one is practice (Abhyasa), and the other is dispassion (Vairagya). Practice implies persistent effort. Engage your mind in a single task; when it wanders, retrieve it. If it strays again, bring it back once more. This repetitive action is crucial, much like a newborn colt that cannot stay still for an instant but constantly roams. Similarly, the mind also ceaselessly drifts. It is as restless as a horse, and controlling such a mind is as challenging as taming a stubborn steed. The more a rider strives to control such a horse, the more it resists and repeatedly attempts to dislodge the rider.
O Krishna, a topic has come up, please tell me: sometimes a person becomes so compelled to commit sin. Who compels him to do so?

Partha, it is his lust (वासना), his inherent self-interest, his anger (क्रोध), and his delusion (मोह) that compel him. Recognize these enemies. Just as smoke covers fire, or dust covers a mirror, or an embryo is enveloped in the womb, so too is knowledge covered by lust (काम), delusion (मोह), and desire (वासना). These are indeed the eternal enemies of the wise. As it is said in the Bhagavad Gita (3.39):
आवृतम् ज्ञानमेतेन ज्ञानिनो नित्यवैरिणा
कामरूपेण कौन्तेय दुष्पूरेणानलेन च
'O son of Kunti, the knowledge of the embodied is covered by this eternal enemy in the form of desire, which is insatiable and burns like fire.' Therefore, make this fire pure, cleanse the mirror, and by subduing your senses, slay these annihilators of knowledge and discrimination.
O Krishna, you speak of a man who is content within himself, beyond joy and sorrow. Who is such a man of steady wisdom (Sthita Prajna), and what are his characteristics?

O Partha, he who abandons all desires that enter the mind, and finds contentment within himself, he is said to be a man of steady wisdom.प्रजहाति यदा कामान् सर्वान् पार्थ मनोगतान् । आत्मन्येवात्मना तुष्टः स्थितप्रज्ञस्तदोच्यते ॥Such a sage maintains equanimity in both pleasure and pain. His words do not spring from the fleeting joys and sorrows of the mind, but from the profound depths of his soul. He speaks the language of detached action, not delusion. When he sits, like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs, he draws his senses within himself, building a fortress within his own being. Indeed, his senses are under his control, and only one whose mind is under control can master his senses.
My mind is often restless, O Krishna. What happens if one's mind and senses are not controlled, and one constantly dwells on worldly objects?

O Partha, when a man constantly contemplates the objects of the senses, attachment to them arises. From attachment comes desire, and from unfulfilled desire, anger is produced.ध्यायतो विषयान् पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते । सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥From anger comes delusion, from delusion the loss of memory, from loss of memory the destruction of intelligence, and from the destruction of intelligence, one perishes.क्रोधाद्भवति सम्मोहः सम्मोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः । स्मृतिभ्रंशाद् बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति ॥Your present delusion, O son of Kunti, is leading you towards such intellectual ruin. How can one find peace without intelligence? One cannot even discern between peace and restlessness. Just as strong winds can carry away a boat on water, desires can lead the mind astray and steal away one's wisdom.इन्द्रियाणां हि चरतां यन्मनोऽनुविधीयते । तदस्य हरति प्रज्ञां वायुर्नावमिवाम्भसि ॥Therefore, O mighty-armed one, keep your senses under your control, and do not become subservient to them.

You spoke of a profound truth, O Krishna, that when the world sleeps, the sage is awake, and when the world wakes, he sleeps. What does this 'sleeping' and 'waking' truly signify? Is it about literal day and night?

I was not speaking of literal day and night, O Partha, but of states of consciousness. The 'waking' state of an ordinary person is spent every moment in the delusion of acquiring and enjoying. This is the sole aim of their consciousness. If they are hungry, they seek food; if thirsty, they seek water; if they desire...
O Krishna, my mind is restless, and my senses pull me in many directions. How can I achieve clarity and act righteously?

Partha, purify your inner mirror and pacify your senses to conquer ignorance and lack of discrimination. As it is said: इन्द्रियाणि पराण्याहुरिन्द्रियेभ्यः परं मनः। मनसस्तु परा बुद्धिर्यो बुद्धेः परतस्तु सः॥ The senses are superior to inert matter, the mind is superior to the senses, the intellect is superior to the mind, and the soul is superior to the intellect. Therefore, O Partha, concern yourself with the soul and strive to rise above the body, senses, mind, and intellect. You are both my devotee and my friend, hence I will reveal to you that eternal Yoga which has long been lost, but which I imparted to Surya at the beginning of creation.
