For, O Partha, ऊर्ध्वमूलमधःशाखमश्वत्थं प्राहुरव्ययम्। छन्दांसि यस्य पर्णानि यस्तं वेद स वेदवित्॥ (Bhagavad Gita 15.1) This world is like an imperishable Ashvattha (Pipal) tree whose roots are upwards and branches downwards. Its leaves are the Vedic hymns. One who knows this tree is the knower of the Vedas. Its branches extend upwards and downwards, nourished by the modes of material nature, with sense objects as their twigs. Its roots are also extended downwards, binding one to fruitive actions in human society.

How is it possible to perform action without desiring its fruits, Vasudeva? Is it not the anticipation of a result that prompts one to act? If our gaze is removed from the outcome, why would anyone act at all?

You ask why anyone would act if not for the fruit, Partha? Life itself is impossible without action! Will you not eat, or will you not feed the hungry? Will you wage war, or will you not? You only have the choice of whether to act or not to act, but the outcome, Partha, the result of action, is not in your control. Your right extends only to the choice of whether to engage in battle or not, but the result of the war is not in your hands. Even if you desire victory, it is not guaranteed; you might also face defeat. However, if you are not enchanted by victory, you will not be afraid of defeat. If you consider, Partha, that whether there is victory or defeat, you are simply performing your duty to fight, then the question of joy in victory or sorrow in defeat does not arise. And one who is neither happy with victory nor distressed by defeat is indeed a Sthitaprajna (one of steady wisdom). Therefore, Partha, do not strive for the fruits of your actions. You must only do what is within your control, that is, fulfill your Dharma. This, Partha, is Karma Yoga. This is Karma Yoga. Understand this secret, Partha: you only have the option to act or not to act, but at the end of the action, the limits of human authority cease. The outcome of action is not within human control. You are the greatest archer, yet if your aim deviates even slightly, you will miss. Your authority is over your aim, your vision, but you have no control over the exact time or the target itself. Indeed, Dhananjaya, noble souls never transgress the limits of their authority. Therefore, remain steadfast in your actions, Partha, remain steadfast, because:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि॥
Your right is to work only, but never to the fruits thereof. Let not the fruits of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction. Strive for efficiency in action.

O Krishna, I am deluded by the world's complexities and seek to understand how one can live a meaningful life and attain lasting peace and liberation in this mortal existence. How can one overcome ignorance and find true wisdom?

Arjuna, a true Karma Yogi performs actions, detached from their fruits, much like a lotus leaf remains untouched by water:
ब्रह्मण्याधाय कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा करोति यः।
लिप्यते न स पापेन पद्मपत्रमिवाम्भसा ॥
Ignorance obscures human knowledge, but self-knowledge destroys this ignorance, illuminating the Supreme Truth like the sun. The wise attain liberation in this very life. This mortal life is crucial; make it purposeful and beneficial for society. Knowledge is light; embrace it to transcend delusion and find peace.
O Dhananjaya, I am the direct path to peace. Those who know Me as the goal of all sacrifices, the Lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, find true peace. If you consider Me your well-wisher, then obey My command and fight. Fleeing your Dharma is not the path to peace. This war is your Dharma; perform it without concern for who wins or loses, for that is not your concern.

O Krishna, you speak of performing Dharma without attachment and renouncing desires. What then is the true meaning of being a Yogi, and how does one achieve such self-mastery, especially in the midst of action like war?

O Pandava, what some call renunciation, you should know as Yoga. Engage in this battle, free from attachment and desire, for without renouncing these, one cannot truly be a Yogi.
One must uplift oneself by oneself; one should not degrade oneself. For the self alone is one's friend, and the self alone is one's enemy:
उद्धरेदात्मनात्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत्।
आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः॥
One who has conquered their mind and senses is their own friend, but one who is enslaved by them is their own enemy. A person who remains calm and balanced in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor, that self-controlled individual is always absorbed in the Supreme. However, this Yoga is not for those who eat too much or too little, sleep excessively or not at all. Life, Arjuna, is about balance, and it is through balanced living that one progresses on the path of Yoga.

O Krishna, you instruct me, "Arjuna, keep your senses under your control, do not become subservient to them." You also speak of a profound difference in perception, saying, "When the world sleeps, the Muni awakens, and when the world awakens, the Muni sleeps." What is this sleeping and waking you speak of? How can day and night be so different for a sage compared to the rest of humanity?

Arjuna, this sleeping and waking is not about literal day and night, but about the state of one's consciousness. Hear this carefully and understand: When the ordinary world is absorbed in the pursuit and enjoyment of material things, fixated on 'getting' and 'consuming'—this is their waking state, their day. If they are hungry, they seek food; if thirsty, water; if exposed to the elements, shelter. Their thought is self-centered, focused only on personal gratification. But for the Muni, the self-controlled sage, that which is 'day' for the ordinary man's senses is 'night'. The Muni’s consciousness is objective, looking beyond individual hunger or thirst. He does not merely think of the fruit on the tree, but of the tree itself, and of the entire forest. Where an ordinary man cuts trees for fuel, the Muni contemplates the importance of forests in nature, their balance, and their relationship with the seasons. Thus, that which is day for the senses of an ordinary man is night for the Muni, for he has transcended the limits of the senses. And that which is night for the senses of an ordinary man is day for the Muni, for in that silence, the sun of the Muni’s consciousness rises. The Muni is interested not only in immediate problems but also in their fundamental solutions, and this distinguishes him from the ordinary man. This truth is captured in the verse:
या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी।
यस्यां जाग्रति भूतानि सा निशा पश्यतो मुनेः॥
Indeed, Arjuna, truth lies beyond the reach of the senses.

O Krishna, I begin to understand this profound difference. But does this mean a Muni does not experience hunger or other bodily desires? How does one who is situated in wisdom deal with these natural urges if truth is beyond the senses?

Arjuna, it is not that a Muni does not feel hunger; indeed, he does. But he sees beyond his personal hunger, contemplating its deeper remedy. While the ordinary man is like a river, carried away by agitation, not knowing its true path, flowing blindly, pouring all its turmoil into the ocean, the Muni is like the ocean itself. Just as the ocean never transgresses the boundaries of its shores, even when receiving countless rivers, so too, the Muni receives the rivers of desires. These desires may sweep away the ordinary man, but when they approach the Muni, he encompasses them without transgressing his own inner boundaries and equipoise. He is not disturbed by the influx of desires, for he is steady, unmoved, and aware of their nature and ultimate solution, remaining established in wisdom.

O Krishna, how can one perform actions in this world without being bound by their outcomes? How can my actions be purified, so I am not tainted by sin, and my life itself becomes beneficial to society?

One who, after completing an action, does not pause in anticipation of its fruit but moves on to another, whose fire of knowledge burns away the impurities of attachment, anger, hatred, desire, gain and loss, joy and sorrow, thus purifying their actions. Their action then becomes non-action (अकर्म), and they, the doer, become a non-doer. Such a knowledgeable one does nothing for themselves beyond securing the essential means of life; their remaining actions are for the welfare of society. This person, while performing actions, is not tainted by sin; their life spontaneously becomes beneficial for society. Hear, O Partha, the life of such an individual is indeed a Yagya. You too, make your life a Yagya, and in its sacrificial fire, burn your desire for the fruits of action, attachment, and anger as offerings.
My Lord, you speak of Yagya, but what exactly is it? For people define sacrifice in many different ways.

O Partha, indeed, different people define Yagya differently. For some, Yagya is the very form of Brahman; for them, everything is Brahman. Some perform Yagya to please the gods; for them, worship is Yagya. Some seekers consider the practice of uniting the individual soul with the Supreme Soul as Yagya. Just like these definitions, the offerings made in them are also of different types: some offer wealth, others offer action. However, in reality, Yagya is of four types: The first is Dravya Yagya (Material Sacrifice), where acquired wealth and resources are used for the welfare of society; this is indeed a public service sacrifice. The second is Tapa Yagya (Ascetic Sacrifice). When one makes their action their penance, their life becomes a sacrifice of austerity. O Partha, performing your Dharma is also a Yagya, but this Dharma is not sectarian; it is Sanatana (eternal), beneficial for both the individual and society. The third Yagya is Yoga Yagya, in which the practice of Ashtanga Yoga is undertaken, and people steadfastly follow the path of meditation and Samadhi, where prana is offered into prana. The fourth Yagya is Gyan Yagya (Knowledge Sacrifice). All four Yagyas are important, O Partha, but the greatest is Gyan Yagya, because it is knowledge that differentiates between good and evil, and by purifying actions in its fire, it makes them auspicious. Knowledge is indeed the pinnacle of excellence in action, and it is knowledge that will free you from the bonds of attachment. O Partha, only the boat of knowledge can cross the ocean of sin. As it is said: श्रेयान् द्रव्यमयाद्यज्ञात् ज्ञानयज्ञः परंतप | सर्वं कर्माखिलं पार्थ ज्ञाने परिसमाप्यते || Better indeed is knowledge-sacrifice than any material sacrifice, O scorcher of foes; for all actions without exception culminate in knowledge, O Partha. ज्ञान ही योग्य ही धर्म है धर्म गुरुओं की आंख कह रही श्री कृष्ण ने अर्जुन से कहा और मानव तुझ से कह रहा हूं कि संसार तेरी कर्मभूमि है और तू अपने कर्मों ही के मानदंड से नापा। The eyes of the gurus of Dharma declare that knowledge is indeed worthy of Dharma. So says Shri Krishna to Arjuna, and to mankind, 'This world is your field of action, and you shall be measured by the standard of your deeds.'

Krishna, my mind is plagued with doubt. How can I bring myself to fight against my own revered elders and relatives on this battlefield? What is the true nature of action (karma), and how can one act without incurring sin, especially when it means facing those I hold dear?

O Partha, do not let your mind be burdened by such thoughts. Just as the ignorant perform actions with attachment to results, so too should the wise act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world. Remember what is said:सक्ताः कर्मण्यविद्वांसो यथा कुर्वन्ति भारत |कुर्याद्विद्वांस्तथासक्तश्चिकीर्षुर्लोकसंग्रहम् ||Ignorant people perform actions driven by self-interest, but the actions of a wise person are selfless, meant for maintaining the balance of the world and for the welfare of all beings. Therefore, surrender your actions to Me and fight this righteous war. On the path of duty, even death becomes auspicious. Even if you must slay your grandfather, gurus, and relatives, you will not incur sin, for performing one's duty is inherently free from sin, Partha, performing one's duty is free from sin. If they attain a valorous death, their demise will be auspicious. And if you attain a valorous death, your death too will be auspicious. Therefore, O Partha, fight! For the path of righteousness can never be the path of sin.
O Krishna, what is the root cause of a man's ruin, and how do desire and attachment lead to such a downfall?

Listen, O Partha, a man's downfall begins with his thoughts.ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते।सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते॥क्रोधाद्भवति सम्मोहः सम्मोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः।स्मृतिभ्रंशाद् बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति॥When a man constantly dwells on the objects of the senses, an attachment to them is formed. From this attachment, desire is born; and from unfulfilled desire, anger arises. From anger, delusion or bewilderment springs forth; from delusion, the loss of memory or discrimination occurs. When memory is lost, the intellect (buddhi) is destroyed, and with the destruction of the intellect, the man perishes completely.O son of Kunti, this very delusion of yours is leading you towards the destruction of your intellect. Reflect, O Partha, how can a person devoid of intellect find peace? He cannot even discern between peace and unrest. And how can one who cannot distinguish peace from unrest ever be truly happy? Just as a strong gust of wind can toss a boat on the waters, so do desires lead the intellect astray.

O Krishna, many describe Yagya (sacrifice) in different ways. Some say it is the form of Brahman, others perform it to please the gods, and some consider the practice of uniting the soul with the Supreme as Yagya. What, then, is the true nature of Yagya, and what are its forms?

Indeed, Partha, people understand Yagya in various ways, and their offerings too differ—some offer wealth, others their actions. However, truly, Yagya is of four principal kinds. The first is Dravya Yagya (Material Sacrifice). In this, accumulated wealth and resources are dedicated to the welfare of society. It is, in essence, a sacrifice of public service. The second is Tapo Yagya (Austerity as Sacrifice). When an individual transforms their actions into their penance, their entire life becomes a Tapo Yagya. O Partha, the adherence to one's Dharma is also a form of Yagya. This Dharma is not sectarian but Sanatana, eternally beneficial for both the individual and society. The third is Yoga Yagya (Yoga as Sacrifice). This involves the practice of Ashtanga Yoga, where devotees dedicate themselves to the path of meditation and Samadhi, offering their vital breaths (pranas) into other pranas. The fourth, and supreme, is Gyana Yagya (Sacrifice of Knowledge). While all four Yagyas are important, Gyana Yagya is the greatest. For it is knowledge that discerns between good and evil, purifying actions by refining them in its fire, making them auspicious. Knowledge is the ultimate pinnacle of excellent action, and it is knowledge alone that will liberate you from the bonds of delusion, O Partha. Only the boat of knowledge can truly cross the ocean of sin. Therefore, perform your actions with the wisdom of knowledge, for supreme knowledge is perseverance, and Karma Yoga is indeed the true Dharma.
O Krishna, the world is full of suffering and delusion. How can one truly overcome the ocean of sin and sorrow?

अपि चेदसि पापेभ्यः सर्वेभ्यः पापकृत्तमः। सर्वं ज्ञानप्लवेनैव वृजिनं संतरिष्यसि॥ (Bhagavad Gita 4.36) Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners, yet you shall cross over all sin by the raft of knowledge alone. Understand, Partha, just as fire reduces everything to ashes, so too does the fire of knowledge burn to ashes the desire for the fruits of action, the anger that arises from not achieving results, and the delusion that grows from that anger. Always remember, O Partha, there is nothing in this world as purifying as knowledge, nor any other element. Knowledge is supreme.
Then, what hinders one from attaining this supreme knowledge, O Krishna, and what is the path to acquiring it?

अज्ञश्चाश्रद्दधानश्च संशयात्मा विनश्यति। नायं लोकोऽस्ति न परो न सुखं संशयात्मनः॥ (Bhagavad Gita 4.40) The ignorant, the faithless, the doubting soul perishes. Neither this world nor the next, nor happiness, is for the doubting soul. Therefore, O Bharata, abandon all doubt and awaken the sage within you. Become a Jnana Yogi, Partha, a Jnana Yogi, and understand that the ultimate stage of knowledge is Karma Sanyasa (the renunciation of action).
But, O Krishna, how can You speak of both Karma Sanyasa and Karma Yoga with such praise? Surely these two paths seem to contradict each other, do they not?

They do not contradict each other, My friend, and both are indeed beneficial. However, among the two, Karma Yoga is superior. He who acts without hatred and desire is a perpetual Sanyasi (renunciate), and being free from both, he is liberated from worldly bonds. Therefore, he who considers Karma Sanyasa and Karma Yoga as separate is indeed foolish; the wise never think so. Renunciation of action, Partha, is essentially the renunciation of inherent selfishness in the path. Hence, Karma Sanyasa cannot be attained without Karma Yoga. A Karma Yogi knows the true principles; his seeing is like not seeing, hearing like not hearing, tasting like not tasting, waking like not waking, taking like not taking, giving up like not giving up, and his every action is for the welfare of the world. Thus, he remains detached from sin, just as a lotus, though in water, remains unaffected by it. ब्रह्मण्याधाय कर्माणि संगं त्यक्त्वा करोति यः। लिप्यते न स पापेन पद्मपत्रमिवाम्भसा॥ (Bhagavad Gita 5.10) He who performs actions, dedicating them to Brahman and abandoning attachment, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not touched by water. The Karma Yogi, by renouncing the fruits of action, attains the Supreme Power and dwells happily in the body, which is like a house with nine gates. The reason for man's delusion, Partha, is that his knowledge often obscures his true knowledge. But when self-knowledge destroys ignorance, that knowledge illuminates the Supreme Reality like the sun. And the wise attain the ultimate truth in this very mortal life.

O Krishna, I am tormented by doubts regarding my duty in this war. My mind is restless, and I yearn for peace and a meaningful existence. How can I achieve these, and what is the true purpose of this mortal life?

O Partha, this mortal life is indeed profoundly significant. Make it purposeful and beneficial for society. Knowledge is light; strive to attain it, and you will transcend the delusions you now face, thereby finding peace. O Dhananjaya, I am the direct path to peace. Those who recognize Me as the ultimate goal of every sacrifice, the supreme Lord of all worlds, and the benevolent friend of all beings, alone find true tranquility. If you consider Me your benefactor, Partha, then obey My command and fight. For without engaging in this battle, you cannot attain peace. To abandon your dharma is not the path to peace. This war is your sacred duty; fulfill it without contemplating the outcomes. Who lives or dies is not your concern. O Pandava, what some call renunciation, you must understand as Yoga, and fight, liberated from all speculative philosophy and desires, for without relinquishing these, one cannot truly be a Yogi.

My Lord, despite understanding my duty, my mind remains uncontrollably restless. How can I restrain it, establish balance in my actions, and achieve the unwavering steadfastness of a Yogi amidst life's challenges?

It is a person's duty to elevate themselves and never to degrade themselves. Indeed, one is one's own friend and also one's own enemy.
उद्धरेदात्मनात्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत्।
आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः॥
One who has conquered their mind and senses becomes their own friend. But one who remains enslaved by them, O Partha, becomes their own foe. That self-controlled individual who maintains calm and balance through cold and heat, joy and sorrow, honor and dishonor, is ever absorbed in the Supreme Self. However, O Partha, this Yoga is not attained by those who eat excessively or too little, or sleep too much or too little. Life is an act of balance, O Partha, and the Yoga of a balanced individual dispels all their sorrows. Just as a lamp's flame remains steady in a windless place, so too does a Yogi, free from delusion, remain unwavering. Do not allow your fickle mind to act whimsically, O Partha; restrain it and bring it under the sway of your Self. This is the remedy for your attachments. Fix your gaze upon Me, O Partha, look towards Me! One who perceives only Me in every direction and in every object can never go astray. One who never forgets Me, O Partha, I also never forget. Even while living a worldly life, they remain separate from the world and abide within My being. O Arjuna, that Yogi is considered supreme who regards the joy and sorrow of all beings as their own, as if they were their own.

O Janardana, my heart is burdened with sorrow and the apprehension of killing those I hold dear. While I do not deny the soul's eternality, ancientness, or indestructibility, I am concerned about these physical bodies. Some bodies are indeed dear to me, like the revered one whose hand often blessed my head and who taught me archery. You say the soul is not born, yet these individuals were born, and their bodies will inevitably perish. How can I not grieve for them, and how can I overcome this attachment and the inevitable sorrow?

O Partha, free yourself from the apprehension of killing or being killed, for death can only be for that which is born. As for happiness and sorrow, O son of Kunti, they come and go like seasons. He who considers both happiness and sorrow equally and endures them without being affected is a man of steady wisdom and is worthy of liberation.मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौंतेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः। आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत।।The soul is timeless, beyond even time. If the soul is not born, how can it die? The soul is unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient, and indestructible. Therefore, O Partha, it is futile to worry about killing or being killed. Death is only for the body, and even after its death, the soul does not die, for:नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः। न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुतः।।For one who is born, O mighty-armed, death is certain. So why grieve for what is certain? One who is born must die one day. And this death is not the end, because the one who dies will be born again. This is an unchangeable truth, O Partha, which no one can avert—neither you, nor I, nor anyone else. Even Bhishma, son of Ganga, who possesses the boon of desired death, cannot escape it.

O Krishna, my heart is overwhelmed with sorrow and confusion. How can I possibly fight against my own kin, my revered gurus, and elders, who stand before me on this battlefield? I see no good in this war; what joy can victory bring when it comes at such a terrible cost?

O Arjuna, how has this impurity come upon you in this moment of crisis? It is unbecoming of a noble person; it leads not to heaven, nor to glory.कश्मलमिदं विषमे समुपस्थितम् अनार्यजुष्टमस्वर्ग्यमकीर्तिकरमर्जुनIn this decisive struggle between Dharma and Adharma, do not be impotent, O Partha! Such unmanliness is unworthy of you, O destroyer of foes. It will cast you down from heaven and deprive you of renown. You yourself will become the cause of your own disgrace. Therefore, cast off this weakness of heart and stand up for battle!

How can I stand to kill my grandfather, Bhishma? How can I raise my weapon against my revered teacher, Dronacharya? They are worthy of my veneration. It would be far better to beg for alms than to enjoy a kingdom stained with the blood of these great souls. O Hrishikesha, I cannot even discern whether victory or defeat is superior in this war. These kings, like my own brothers, stand before me. How can I live if I kill them? It will not be easy to win after slaying them, O Keshava! Are they not my brothers?

You have only asked this, O Partha. But this war is not for establishing or identifying relationships. O son of Kunti, recognize your duty and then make your decision, for the decision must be yours alone. If you wish that I make the decision, and thus escape the responsibility of this war, that will not happen, O Partha, never will it happen! For this war is yours, and its outcome will also be yours.

O Keshava, I cannot clearly see the path of duty. Therefore, O Vasudeva, please become the charioteer of my soul. I know that I stand between Dharma and Adharma, but I cannot decide which way Dharma lies, or which way Adharma. I seek your guidance; show me the path to avoid the grief that dries up the senses. In this state of mind, O Govinda, I cannot fight.

O Krishna, my mind is filled with despair. How can I bring myself to fight against my own relatives, my teachers, my friends? I see no good in this war, neither in victory nor in defeat. I fear the immense sin of slaying these great warriors, and I am uncertain of what is right for me to do. My heart falters at the thought of the sorrow and destruction that will ensue.

O Partha, your reputation will be destroyed, and if that happens, not only your adversaries but society as a whole will brand you a cowardly person, and coming generations will consider you timid and sinful. Therefore, O mighty-armed one, do not dwell on questions of victory and defeat, life and death, pleasure and pain, but fight! For if you achieve victory in this battle, you will enjoy the kingdom of the earth and its glory; and if you attain martyrdom, you will still achieve fame along with heaven. Therefore, O son of Kunti, arise! Treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal, and engage in battle! This is both your Kshatriya duty and your human dharma. अथवा प्राप्स्यसि स्वर्गं जित्वा वा भोक्ष्यसे महीम् तस्मादुत्तिष्ठ कौंतेय युद्धाय कृतनिश्चयः This means, 'Either slain you will attain heaven, or victorious you will enjoy the earth; therefore, arise, O son of Kunti, resolved to fight.' Remember, the soul does not truly die; it is eternal and imperishable.
I grieve, O Krishna, at the thought of slaying my own kin and respected elders. How can I bring myself to fight against them?

Indeed, Partha, those who have passed are gone. The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead. They lament neither for what is past nor for what is yet to come. Your understanding is that of the wise, yet you speak like the foolish. Before grieving, consider this: those for whom you lament are not worthy of such sorrow.
Then, O Keshav, are revered figures like Grandfather Bhishma and Guru Drona not worthy of grief?

If they were worthy of grief, then I would tell you so, O Bharata. Understand this truth, Partha: the fundamental essence is not the body, but the soul. Death is not the end of its journey, for its journey is eternal. Death is merely a temporary stop, Partha, just a pause. The cessation of breath is not the cessation of the life force. Understand it thus, Partha: a being is first a child, then that child becomes a youth, then that youth becomes old, and then comes death. But this journey is of the body; the soul goes even further than this. It discards one body and assumes another. Therefore, the journey that ends with death is merely the journey of the body, Partha, only the journey of the body.न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः। अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे॥ The journey of the soul is eternal, Partha. At one point in its journey, the body is left behind, and the traveler moves forward. It takes on a new garment just as we cast off old clothes and put on new ones.वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि। तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णान्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही॥O Partha, destruction cannot touch the soul. So, what sort of grief is this for the destruction of anyone? Is it for the destruction of clothes? But clothes are not truly 'ours'; they are meant to be cast off. And the soul does not die, never dies.
But these very people standing before me, will they not all be utterly destroyed after this war? Will they all not cease to exist?

What is this 'being' and 'non-being', Partha? For there never was a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor all these kings. And there will never be a time in the future when I will cease to exist, or you, or all these kings. Then why are you caught in the illusion, Partha, that this present life is the complete life? This current life is not the complete life, Partha. We have always existed.
I have brought you here to ask what my duty and Dharma are.

Then, O Partha, where is the place for sorrow in the chain of birth, death, and rebirth? Those people whom you see standing before you, O Partha, existed before this birth as well, but what that was, you do not know. They will exist after this birth as well, but what they will be, you also do not know. Their existence is not confined to these two points of birth and death, or if it is, it is unknown, unmanifest. That is, before this birth, they were not for you, O Partha, and they will not be after this birth either. So, O Partha, for those whose life's essential component is death, and whose inevitable end you can neither postpone nor change, then why sorrow? Why lament? You did not know any of these grandfathers, these teachers, these relatives before this birth, O Partha, nor will you know them after this birth. So then, to grieve for them would indeed be futile, O Partha, futile.
अव्यक्तादीनि भूतानि व्यक्तमध्यानि भारत।अव्यक्तनिधनान्येव तत्र का परिदेवना॥
(Unmanifest at their beginning, manifest in their middle state, and unmanifest again at their end are all beings, O Bharata. What then is there to lament about?)What is surprising in this, O Partha? Just as an old garment is ultimately discarded, so too is death the ultimate truth of the body. Why then lament over truth? This human body is not a mixture of the perishable and the imperishable; the body is merely a means for the soul. Therefore, one should continue to perform one's Dharma without worrying about the body. But even if you are thinking about your Kshatriya Dharma, O Partha, you should still do what is right. Because taking up arms against unrighteousness is the Dharma of a Kshatriya. And those who have taken up arms against Dharma stand before you. Therefore, O Partha, fulfill your Kshatriya Dharma. Is that clear?
स्वधर्ममपि चावेक्ष्य न विकम्पितुमर्हसि।धर्म्याद्धि युद्धाच्छ्रेयोऽन्यत्क्षत्रियस्य न विद्यते॥
(Considering your own duty as well, you should not waver, for there is nothing more auspicious for a warrior than a righteous war.)
And who are you, O Partha? Who are you yourself?
I am Arjuna, the disciple of Drona. What, am I nothing more than that? I am Arjuna, son of Kunti. And I am a Kshatriya, Keshava.

If you were not a Kshatriya, O Partha, you would not be Drona's disciple. And who are you? Even as Kunti's son, you are a Kshatriya. So, all three of your identities are Kshatriya identities. Therefore, Kshatriya Dharma is your Dharma. Follow this Dharma. To raise arms against unrighteousness is the Kshatriya Dharma. To raise arms against injustice and immorality is the Kshatriya Dharma. And if, in this decisive moment, you do not take up arms in favor of truth and against untruth, O Partha, then along with your Dharma, your glorious reputation...
But, Keshav, you have taken birth in this modern age, while Surya Dev (the Sun God) is ancient. How can I believe that you imparted this Yoga to Surya Dev at the very beginning of creation?

बहूनि मे व्यतीतानि जन्मानि तव चार्जुन। तान्यहं वेद सर्वाणि न त्वं वेत्थ परंतप॥ Yes, Partha, both you and I have passed through many births. I remember all of them, but you, O scorcher of foes (Parantapa), do not. Though I am unborn, imperishable, and the Lord of all beings, I manifest Myself by controlling My own material nature through My Yogamaya (divine mystic power). Whenever and wherever there is a decline in righteousness and an increase in unrighteousness, O descendant of Bharata (Arjuna), I manifest Myself. परित्राणाय साधूनाम् विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम्। धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे॥ To deliver the pious, to annihilate the miscreants, and to reestablish the principles of Dharma, I appear millennium after millennium. Thus, I manifest myself, I come when Dharma declines, when unrighteousness increases. I come to protect the virtuous, to destroy the wicked, and to establish Dharma, taking birth in every age.
I am troubled, O Janardana. My heart is heavy seeing my kin arrayed against me. How can I fight them? Is this present life truly all there is? It seems so complete to me.

Why do you fall into this delusion, Partha, that the present life is the entirety of existence? The present life is not the complete life. We are, and we shall be. As for these joys and sorrows, what are they, son of Kunti? He who regards both joy and sorrow with equanimity, and endures them without being affected, is a person of steady wisdom (Sthita-pragya) and alone is qualified for liberation. मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः | आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत || Be free from the apprehension of dying or not dying, for death can only befall that which is born – the living being, not the soul. If the soul is never born, how can it die? The soul simply exists, Partha; it is eternal in the flow of time, immutable, indestructible. Therefore, it is futile to worry about the question of dying or not dying, Partha, it is futile. Death only pertains to the body, and even after its death, the soul does not die, for weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, and wind cannot dry it.

But Janardana, my concern is not just for the soul. Do I call only a soul my Grandsire Bhishma? I used to spend my days in the lap of a soul, dressed in clothes soiled with dust. Did not the body, which you call the garment of the soul, countless times place its hand on my head to bless me? Is that venerable, best of Brahmins who taught me knowledge, merely a soul, Keshava? I do not deny the soul's eternality, its ancientness, its indestructibility. But the bodies I speak of, those bodies are also dear to me, are they not? The soul may not take birth, but people do take birth, Keshava.

Indeed, people take birth, Partha. But take this thought a little further, O Mighty-armed. He who is born, his death is certain. So why grieve for that which is certain? One who is born must die one day, and this death is not the end, for the one who dies will be reborn. This is an unshakeable truth, Partha, and no one can avert this unshakeable truth – neither you, nor I, nor anyone else. Even Bhishma has the boon of 'Ichha Mrityu' (death at will), yet death is still inevitable. Where then, is the place for sorrow in this cycle of death and then rebirth, Bharata? Where is the place for sorrow? The people whom you see standing before you, Partha, existed even before this birth, but what they were, you do not know. They will exist even after this birth, but what they will be, you also do not know. Their existence beyond these two points of birth and death is either non-existent for you, or if it is, it is unknown, unmanifest. That is to say, before this birth, they were not there for you, Partha, and after this birth, they also will not be. For those whose life has an inevitable end and an unknown beginning and future, why do you grieve, Partha?

Keshav, how can I fight them? My revered grandfather, Bhishma, and my esteemed guru, Dronacharya, stand before me. He is my grandfather, who loved me dearly; he is my guru, who bathed my soul in his ocean of knowledge and poured all his wisdom into this disciple's lap. My Gandiva is slipping from my hand. My hair stands on end just to honor them! I cannot turn this battlefield of Kurukshetra into a cremation ground for my own family, nor can I build my kingdom upon their ashes. What good is a kingdom that smells of the blood of my own kin? How can I aim arrows at those revered teachers at whose feet I placed my head, those who taught me how to wield a bow? I do not desire victory over these esteemed ones. I concede that Duryodhana has deceived us and dishonored Panchali, thereby insulting the entire Bharata clan. But isn't it lamentable that for a mere piece of land, we are ready to become slayers of our own? If, by losing everything, I can find peace and avoid the sin of destroying my lineage, then that peace is very cheap, Keshav. It is far better to extend my hands for alms than to raise them against these great personalities. The bread received as alms would not be stained with their blood. Is victory or defeat truly superior in this war? The sons of Dhritarashtra stand before me like enemies. I know it's impossible to live without killing them, but Keshav, even after killing them, to live...

O Arjuna, before you utter my name, tell me, Partha, when the clouds of destruction have gathered all around, and the banner of Dharma's protection and victory awaits you, how did you allow such lowly feelings of cowardice to enter your heart in this hour of crisis? Noble men do not succumb to such despondency. In this decisive moment of conflict between Dharma and Adharma, do not be impotent, Partha, do not be impotent! Therefore, O Partha, these ignoble feelings, unworthy of an Arya, will neither lead you to heaven nor bring you fame. Do not yield to impotence, O son of Pṛthā; it does not befit you. Abandon this petty weakness of heart and arise, O vanquisher of foes!कुतस्त्वा कश्मलमिदं विषमे समुपस्थितम्।अनार्यजुष्टमस्वर्ग्यमकीर्तिकरमर्जुन॥२-२॥क्लैब्यं मा स्म गमः पार्थ नैतत्त्वय्युपपद्यते।क्षुद्रं हृदयदौर्बल्यं त्यक्त्वोत्तिष्ठ परंतप॥२-३॥

Keshav, how can this be easy? Are they not my brothers? Tell me, is it truly necessary? I stand bewildered between Dharma and Adharma, unable to decide which path is righteous. Please become the charioteer of my soul and guide me. In this mental state, I cannot fight, Govinda. I cannot fight.

O son of Kunti, recognize your duty and then decide, for the decision must be yours. This war is yours, and its outcome will also be yours. You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, yet speak words of wisdom. The truly wise lament neither for the living nor for the dead. The fundamental reality is not the body, but the soul. Death is but a transition, not the end of its journey, for its journey is eternal. Just as a person discards worn-out clothes and dons new ones, the embodied soul casts off old bodies and enters new ones.वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि।तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णान्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही॥ (Bhagavad Gita 2.22)The soul, O Bhārata, cannot be touched by destruction. It is immortal, never truly dying.
But Keshav, are not grandsire Bhishma and our revered teacher Drona worthy of grief? Are they not mortal?

If they were truly worthy of such grief, I would not say this. It is not that you, or I, or these kings have never existed, nor will it be that we shall cease to exist in the future. The soul is eternal; it never truly perishes.

O Keshava, when I see my own kinsmen, revered elders, and teachers standing before me, ready for battle, my limbs fail, my mouth dries up, and my heart sinks with sorrow. How can I possibly fight against those I hold dear? My mind is utterly confused as to what is right.

O Partha, why do you grieve for that which is inevitable? Death is the ultimate truth for the body, just as decay is for a garment. You knew none of these relatives before their birth, nor will you know them after their death. Why, then, lament for them? It is futile, Partha, utterly futile.अव्यक्तदीनि भूतानि व्यक्तमध्यानि भारत। अव्यक्तनिधनान्येव तत्र का परिदेवना।।The human being is not merely this perishable body; the soul is imperishable. Therefore, without worrying about the body, one should continue to perform their dharma. But even if you consider your Kshatriya dharma, Partha, you must still fight. For it is the dharma of a Kshatriya to raise weapons against unrighteousness. Today, unrighteousness stands arrayed against dharma. Therefore, O Bharata, fulfill your Kshatriya dharma.
O Keshava, it is precisely to ask you this that I have brought you here: What is my duty? What is my dharma, Keshava?
And who are you, Partha? Who do you truly believe yourself to be?
I am Drona's disciple, Arjuna. Is there nothing more? I am Kunti's son, Arjuna. And... and I am a Kshatriya.

If you were not a Kshatriya, Partha, you would not be Drona's disciple. And as Kunti's son, you are also a Kshatriya. Thus, all three of your identities confirm that Kshatriya dharma is your dharma. Fulfill that dharma. To raise arms against adharma is the Kshatriya dharma. To raise arms against injustice and unrighteousness is the Kshatriya dharma. And if, in this decisive moment, you do not wield your weapons in favor of truth and against untruth, Partha, then along with your dharma, your bright renown will also be destroyed. If this happens, Partha, not only your enemies but society as a whole will brand you as a tainted coward, and future generations will consider you timid and sinful. Therefore, O Kunti's son, do not be entangled in questions of victory and defeat, life and death, pleasure and sorrow, but fight! If you are victorious in this war, you will enjoy the kingdom of the Earth and fame. And if you attain a hero's death, you will achieve heaven along with fame. Therefore, O Kaunteya, resolve this within yourself. The soul does not die; it is eternal. Do not keep any doubt or hesitation in your mind.
